project_description: The requirements definition of OpenV itself: multi-agent development suite, multi-tenant SaaS, predictable BYO-AI execution.

artifacts.title: Partial-reply pump and single-flight guided nudges
artifacts.body:
How REQ-119 is built.

**Reply text on its way to the browser.** The Claude adapter reads the CLI's
`stream-json` output and accumulates assistant text deltas; the runner's
existing log pump, which already posts to `POST /agent-runs/{id}/logs` every
750 ms, carries the text written so far as a `partial_text` field, rate
limited to one report per second. A CLI that emits no incremental text (the
Codex path) reports its last complete agent message instead, so the field is
always the best text available rather than a guess. The adapter probes the
CLI's streaming support once behind a mutex holding a tri-state result, so a
probe that fails is retried rather than latched off.

`AppendAgentRunLogs` stores the latest partial on the run, and the
orchestration hook broadcasts `assistant_partial` on the session's stream at
most twice per second per run. `GuidedChatPanel` renders the growing text and
replaces it with the final message when the run finishes.

**The partial is never left behind.** Migration 0027 adds `partial_text` to
`agent_runs`, and every path that ends a run clears it: completion,
abandonment, `FailStale` on a dead run, and `ReleaseClaim` on one that is
re-queued. A partial from a previous attempt therefore cannot surface as the
reply to a later one.

**One turn per nudge.** `NudgeGuidedChat` records a pending nudge on the
session rather than launching a second turn while one is in flight, keeping
the latest state; the take-back parks the nudge and then re-checks the run,
which closes the race where a turn finishes between the check and the park.
When the turn finishes, the hook launches exactly one turn with the held
nudge, guarded by the session's status so a nudge parked against a session
that has since been committed or abandoned is dropped rather than launched.
Commit and abandon clear `pending_nudge` for the same reason. The frontend
defers on the trailing edge, so the newest nudge is the one that survives the
throttle instead of the oldest.

artifacts.title: Shared-product votes and the Top 5 filters
artifacts.body:
How REQ-118 is built.

**Storage.** Migration 0028 adds `shared_product_votes`, one row per member
per product, with a denormalised `vote_count` on `shared_products` so a list
costs one query. `changeVote` opens its transaction with
`SELECT hidden FROM shared_products WHERE id = $1 FOR UPDATE`, which takes
the row lock and answers the visibility question in the same statement: two
members voting at once serialise on that lock, so the recount cannot run on a
stale snapshot and leave the count behind the vote rows. A hidden product is
refused there, before any vote row is written.

**The starter pool.** `internal/seeds/product_concepts.go` holds fifteen
concepts, each with one canonical name and one fixed vision, written out in
full rather than assembled at render time — a product that renders under a
different name each roll has no identity to attach a vote to.
`EnsureSharedProductPool` publishes them at boot through
`sharedproducts.Sanitize`, the same validation the publish endpoint applies,
so a starter entry cannot carry anything a member would be refused for.

Seeding is idempotent by the pool's existing rule rather than a new one: the
UNIQUE index on the normalised `name_key` makes a repeat boot a no-op, and
makes a member's own entry win — the seed fills a gap, it never overwrites
somebody's row. It runs once at boot rather than per workspace, because the
pool is one list the whole deployment reads, and it is best-effort: an
unseeded pool is duller, not broken, so a failure is logged and the server
starts. Seeded rows carry no `created_by_user`, which is how moderation tells
an authored entry from a starter one.

**The two leaderboards.** All-time orders by the denormalised count. The
weekly board counts vote rows inside a window built from `VoteWindowDays` with
`make_interval(days => $n)`, so the constant is the single source of the
window and moving it moves both the query and the label. Both exclude hidden
products, and both cap at five.

**Voting identity.** A vote belongs to a member, so the handler requires a
user session; a runner key carries no member and is refused.

**The picker.** The random-product control offers the three filters as a
segmented control. Each fetch carries a sequence number and a late response
from a filter the member has already moved off is discarded, in the failure
path as well as the success path, so a slow earlier request cannot overwrite
the rows of the filter now shown. The roller draws from the shared pool and
this browser's unpublished inventions; the client-side concepts join the roll
only when the pool came back empty, since rendering one that is also a seeded
row would put an unvotable twin of the same product in the roll. The vote
control names why it is disabled when it is: a built-in example shown as a
fallback and an invention kept only in this browser are different cases, and
the card is given the kept inventions at render time so it can tell them
apart.

artifacts.title: Streamed replies arrive, die with their run, and nudges launch one turn
artifacts.body:
Verifies REQ-119. Automated; `go test ./internal/...` with a Postgres test
database, plus the frontend suite.

1. **Deltas become partial text.** `internal/runner/claudecode_test.go` and
   `partial_stream_test.go` feed `stream-json` output to the adapter and assert
   the accumulated assistant text, the one-per-second report rate, and the
   Codex path reporting its last complete agent message. A failing streaming
   probe is retried on the next run rather than latching the feature off.
2. **The API stores and broadcasts it.** `internal/api/run_partial_text_test.go`
   posts logs carrying `partial_text`, asserts the run holds the latest, and
   asserts the `assistant_partial` broadcast is capped at twice per second per
   run.
3. **A partial never outlives its run.** `internal/persistence/postgres/partial_text_test.go`
   asserts the column is cleared on completion, on abandonment, by `FailStale`
   on a dead run, and by `ReleaseClaim` on a re-queued one.
4. **One turn per held nudge.** `internal/api/guided_nudge_test.go` and
   `internal/orchestration/hooks_test.go` assert a nudge arriving mid-turn is
   held rather than launched, that the latest state wins, that exactly one turn
   launches when the running turn finishes, that a turn finishing during the
   park is not missed, and that a nudge parked against a committed or abandoned
   session is dropped.
5. **The panel renders the growing reply** and replaces it with the final
   message (frontend suite).

Pass: every assertion above holds and the full Go and frontend suites are
green.

artifacts.title: One vote per member, counted under lock, and the two Top 5 boards
artifacts.body:
Verifies REQ-118. Automated; `go test ./internal/...` with a Postgres test
database, the frontend suite, and the layout audit.

1. **One vote, withdrawable.** `internal/persistence/postgres/shared_product_repository_test.go`
   asserts a second vote from the same member does not double the count and
   that withdrawing returns it.
2. **The recount cannot lose a vote.** The same file drives concurrent vote
   changes against one product and asserts the denormalised count equals the
   number of vote rows afterwards, which the `FOR UPDATE` row lock guarantees.
3. **Hidden is refused everywhere.** A hidden product is absent from the pool,
   from both leaderboards, and voting on it is not found
   (`TestVoteHiddenSharedProductIsNotFound`).
4. **A runner key holds no vote.** `TestVoteSharedProductNeedsAPerson` asserts
   the handler refuses a caller with no member.
5. **The window follows the constant.** A test moves `VoteWindowDays` and
   asserts the weekly board's boundary moves with it, so the interval cannot
   drift from the label.
6. **The starter pool fills, once.** `internal/seeds/shared_products_test.go`
   asserts an empty pool receives every starter entry, that a second run adds
   nothing, that a member's row published under the same name survives
   untouched, that every entry passes the publish validation and carries a
   distinct normalised name, and that a failing repository is reported without
   stopping the boot.
   `internal/persistence/postgres/shared_product_seed_test.go` repeats the
   first two against the real table — where the UNIQUE index on `name_key` is
   what makes the repeat a no-op — and asserts the seeded rows list like any
   other and that one of them can be voted for.
7. **The picker.** The frontend suite asserts the three filters, that a late
   response from an abandoned filter is discarded in both the success and the
   failure path, that the disabled vote control names the right reason for a
   built-in example and for an invention kept only in this browser, and that
   the roller draws only from the pool while the pool is non-empty, falling
   back to the client-side concepts only when it is empty.
8. **Layout.** The audit renders the project list and the Top 5 picker across
   the android, iphone and desktop profiles with no overflow, clipping or
   undersized target.

Pass: every assertion above holds, the suites are green, and the audit reports
no finding.

artifacts.title: Archived notifications, flags, and keyset-paged views
artifacts.body:
How REQ-120 is built.

**Archive, not delete.** Migration 0029 adds `cleared_at` (NULL while a
notification is in the inbox) and `flagged` to `notifications`.
`POST /api/v1/notifications/clear` stamps `cleared_at` and marks the row read;
the rows move between views rather than going anywhere, which is what makes a
history possible at all. It is a POST for that reason —
`DELETE /api/v1/notifications/cleared` is the one path that destroys a
notification, and it can only reach rows the member has already put aside.

**Three views, one query.** `ListQuery` carries the view, so the same statement
serves all three: the inbox is `cleared_at IS NULL`, the history is
`cleared_at IS NOT NULL`, and the flagged view is `flagged` regardless of
either. Two partial indexes cover the two hot ones — `(user_id, created_at
DESC) WHERE cleared_at IS NULL` and `... WHERE flagged`; the history is the
rarely-opened view and rides the existing user index.

**Flags are independent of clearing.** Flagging does not exempt a row from a
clear. It means the flagged view still finds the row afterwards, so a clear
needs no special case and nothing is stranded — and flagging from the cleared
view is how a member pulls something back out of the history.
`PUT /api/v1/notifications/{id}/flag` scopes the update by session user, so an
id belonging to someone else matches nothing and answers 404: the same answer
a missing id gets, which is what stops the endpoint confirming that a
notification exists.

**Keyset paging.** `?before=<created_at>|<id>` rather than an offset, because
the history grows at the top: an offset would skip or repeat rows as
notifications arrive between pages. The id is half the key on purpose — a
fan-out writes several rows in the same instant, and `created_at` alone cannot
order them stably. A response carries `next_cursor` only when the page came
back full, so the client stops asking at the end.

**The badge.** `CountUnread` is scoped to the inbox, so a cleared row never
keeps it lit however it was left. The panel's SSE handler prepends an arriving
notification only while the inbox is the view showing, so a new row cannot
appear in a list it does not belong to.

artifacts.title: Clearing archives, flags survive it, and the history pages cleanly
artifacts.body:
Verifies REQ-120. Automated; `go test ./internal/...` with a Postgres test
database, the frontend suite, and the layout audit.

1. **Clearing archives.** `internal/persistence/postgres/notification_repository_test.go`
   clears an inbox holding read and unread rows, then asserts the inbox is
   empty, the unread count is zero, and every row is in the cleared view with
   a `cleared_at` stamp — nothing was destroyed.
2. **One member's clear spares another's.** The same test asserts a second
   member's notifications are untouched by both the clear and the purge.
3. **The purge is the only destructive path.** It deletes the cleared rows and
   leaves everyone else's alone; clearing an empty inbox is a no-op.
4. **A flag survives a clear.** `TestNotificationRepositoryFlagging` flags a
   row, clears the inbox, and asserts the flagged view still returns it with
   its `cleared_at` set — flagging does not exempt it, it makes it findable.
   Unflagging removes it from the view.
5. **A flag reaches only the member's own rows.** Flagging another member's id
   matches nothing and reports not-found, and the handler turns that into 404
   — the same answer a missing id gets.
6. **Paging returns each row exactly once.** `TestNotificationRepositoryCursorPaging`
   inserts rows of which three deliberately share a timestamp, pages through
   with a limit below the total, and asserts every row appeared once and none
   twice — which the `(created_at, id)` keyset gives and `created_at` alone
   could not.
7. **The API carries the view and the cursor.** `internal/api/notification_handlers_test.go`
   asserts the view and cursor reach the service, a malformed cursor is a 400
   rather than a silent first page, an unknown view falls back to the inbox so
   an older client keeps working, and every endpoint is refused without a
   session user.
8. **The panel.** The frontend suite asserts the three tabs switch, each bulk
   action appears only on the view it acts on, clearing says where the
   notifications went while deleting warns it cannot be undone, flagging is
   optimistic and reverts on failure, and Load older pages with the cursor the
   server returned.
9. **Layout.** The audit renders the notifications panel across the android,
   iphone and desktop profiles with no overflow, clipping or undersized
   target.

Pass: every assertion above holds, the suites are green, and the audit reports
no finding.

artifacts.title: Test evidence capture for physical and manual verification
artifacts.body: The system shall store test evidence as a capture session that belongs to a project. The system shall allow any number of recorded test results to cite one capture session. The system shall give each capture session a citable reference and shall never reissue that reference. Each capture session shall hold a description of what the tester did and observed. Each capture session shall also hold the capture date, the name of the tester, and the files the tester uploads. The system shall keep a citation intact when a user re-records the cited result. The system shall serve every uploaded evidence file as a download that no browser renders. The system shall reject an upload that takes the workspace past its evidence storage limit. The system shall state the amount of storage in use when it rejects such an upload.

artifacts.title: Evidence bundles, files and citations
artifacts.body:
Three tables (migration 0030). evidence_bundles is the capture session, owned by the project rather than by a run, because one session on a rig commonly answers several test cases and may still stand when the campaign is repeated. evidence_files holds the uploaded data, deliberately separate from attachments: an attachment is a numbered figure that must hang off an artifact and must be an image. evidence_citations is the many-to-many.

A citation targets test_results.id rather than a test case. That id survives a re-record, because the result upsert is ON CONFLICT (run_id, test_case_id) DO UPDATE, which is the property the previous evidence array on the result lacked — it was rewritten on every upsert, so editing a note discarded it.

Bundle references (EVD-1) come from artifact_ref_counters, the existing per-project counter, so the workspace-deletion sweep that clears those clears these too, and no number is ever reissued.

Uploads are a second path beside the figure one: any format, streamed to disk through a SHA-256 rather than buffered, capped per file by OPENV_MAX_EVIDENCE_MB and per workspace by the evidence_storage_mb org limit. Downloads are always application/octet-stream with Content-Disposition: attachment, nosniff and default-src 'none', because evidence may be any format including ones that carry script. The workspace quota is a hazard control: uploads share the deployment's single volume, so an uncapped campaign could exhaust it.

Agents may read bundles but not create them, matching the existing rule that an agent cannot record a result for a physical or manual test case.

artifacts.title: Evidence capture, citation and storage limits
artifacts.body:
Covers REQ-121.

1. One capture, several cases. Create a bundle in a project, upload a file, and cite it from the results of three different test cases in one run. Expect the bundle to report three citations, each carrying its test case and run name, and the run's citation map to return one entry per result.
2. A citation survives a re-record. Cite a bundle from a result, then re-record that result with a different status and notes. Expect the result id to be unchanged and the citation, including its note, still present.
3. Citing twice is quiet. Cite the same bundle from the same result twice. Expect one citation and no error.
4. Uncite keeps the capture. Remove one of three citations. Expect the bundle to still exist with the other two.
5. Delete is the destructive path. Delete a bundle that has files and a citation. Expect the file rows returned for unlinking, the bundle unreadable, and no orphaned citation.
6. Storage. With 60 MB of evidence in a workspace, expect a 50 MB limit to reject any upload, a 100 MB limit to accept 30 MB and reject 50 MB, and an unlimited setting to accept anything. Expect the refusal to name the amount in use.
7. References ascend per project and are never reissued, including after the newest bundle is deleted.
8. Evidence is preserved. Recording a result without an evidence field leaves the existing evidence alone; an explicit empty list clears it.
9. Downloads. Upload a file declared text/html and fetch it. Expect application/octet-stream, Content-Disposition: attachment, nosniff, a default-src 'none' policy, and the recorded digest in X-Evidence-SHA256.
10. Upload limits. Expect a file over OPENV_MAX_EVIDENCE_MB to be refused, and the evidence cap to be independent of the figure cap.

artifacts.title: Notification of membership and privilege changes
artifacts.body: The system shall notify a member when it changes their access to a workspace or a project. The notification shall state the access the member holds after the change. The system shall notify every workspace administrator when a person joins the workspace, leaves it, receives an invitation to it, or changes workspace role. The system shall name the person and both the previous and the new role when it reports a role change. The system shall omit the person who performed a change from the recipients of every notification it sends for that change. The system shall omit a member who left of their own accord from the recipients of the departure notification. The system shall notify administrators alone when it invites an address that holds no account.

artifacts.title: Membership events and the two-audience fan-out
artifacts.body:
Eight new bus events (org.member_added, _role_changed, _removed, org.invitation_sent, _accepted, and the three project equivalents) published from the handlers that make the change. The workspace ones carry no ProjectID; Event.OrgID is stamped with WithOrg, and publishOrgEvent passes the workspace explicitly because the acting user's active workspace is not necessarily the one being edited. publishOrgEventAs serves the paths with no request to read an actor from, such as an invitation taken up during an OIDC sign-in.

Two notification types, because the audiences and the reasons differ. access_changed answers "what can I do now?" for the affected member and states the resulting access rather than the transition. membership_changed is workspace governance for the admins, and carries both ends of a role change.

The fan-out reuses what already existed: notify.Notifier gains an OrgMemberLister and a UserNamer, and alertOrgAdmins mirrors the budget monitor's admin fan-out. deliver already skips the event's actor, which is what keeps a person from being told what they just did; the acceptance paths therefore name the joining user as actor.

Scoping decisions: project membership changes reach the member but not workspace admins, because project roles change constantly and would bury the arrivals and departures that matter; a member who left of their own accord is not told they left, though the admins are, worded as a departure rather than a removal; an invited address with no account has nobody to notify in app, so the invitation email is that person's notification and only the admins get a row, with a second one on acceptance. Both types are in DefaultEmailTypes because an access change matters most when the person is not looking at the app.

artifacts.title: Membership and privilege notification fan-out
artifacts.body:
Covers REQ-122. Workspace under test: two admins (alice, carol) and a member (bob).

1. Role change. Alice promotes Bob. Expect Bob to get one access_changed saying he is now an admin; Carol one membership_changed naming Bob, the new role and the previous one; Alice nothing.
2. Scope. Alice adds Dave. Expect Dave one access_changed, Carol one membership_changed, and Bob (an ordinary member) nothing.
3. Removal by another person. Alice removes Bob. Expect Bob to be told he was removed, and Carol to be told he was removed.
4. Voluntary departure. Bob removes himself. Expect Bob nothing, and Carol one notification worded as leaving rather than removal.
5. Invitation to an address with no account. Expect exactly one notification, to the non-acting admin, naming the invited address. Nothing is sent to the invitee.
6. Acceptance. Dave accepts. Expect both admins to be told he joined, and Dave nothing.
7. Project scope. A project role change for Bob. Expect Bob one access_changed naming the new project role with an entity ref of kind project_membership, and workspace admins nothing.
8. No workspace roster configured. Expect only the affected member to be notified, rather than a half-delivered fan-out.
9. Unknown display name. Expect the admin copy to fall back to a readable word rather than putting a raw user id in front of a person.
10. Email defaults. Expect access_changed and membership_changed both to appear in DefaultEmailTypes.

artifacts.title: Workspace limits and their refusals
artifacts.body:
The system shall resolve each workspace limit from the workspace's own setting, then the deployment's setting, then the plan's default. The system shall treat a limit of zero as no ceiling. The system shall let an operator set any limit for a whole deployment through configuration. The system shall apply no ceiling to any workspace when the operator configures the deployment as self-hosted, whatever plan the workspace holds. The system shall allow exactly one member in a personal workspace, whatever the plan, the deployment setting and the workspace setting hold. The system shall report every limit and its usage to any member of the workspace. The system shall mark a limit that no plan and no setting raises, so that a reader can tell a fact from a warning. The system shall state the limit, the amount allowed and the amount used when it refuses an action. The system shall tell a member of a hosted workspace to upgrade the plan, and shall tell a member of a self-hosted deployment which setting to change. The system shall tell a member who tries to add a person to a personal workspace to create a shared workspace. The system shall count invitations that nobody has accepted towards the workspace member limit. The system shall keep every existing member, project and file when a workspace passes a limit.

A published tier that presents itself as containing another tier shall grant more than that other tier. The system shall set every resource limit on such a tier's plan above the same limit on the contained tier's plan.

artifacts.title: Three-layer limit resolution with a structural seat
artifacts.body:
A single catalogue in the orgs domain names every limit, its label, its unit and whether its usage can be counted. The docs, the limits endpoint and the settings panel all render from it, so a limit cannot be added and left undocumented.

A value resolves through three layers, most specific first: the workspace's own limits column, then the deployment's OPENV_LIMITS, then the plan's defaults. Zero means no ceiling uniformly, for every key. OPENV_SELF_HOSTED bases the resolution on the self-host plan whatever the stored plan says, so a deployment somebody runs themselves lifts the ceilings on workspaces created before the operator set it. A malformed OPENV_LIMITS fails the boot rather than being ignored, because a typo that silently did nothing would look exactly like a limit that does not work.

The plan defaults are a ladder, and the tiers are sold as one: Business is presented as everything in Business Lite and more. Until issue #361 every cloud-runner figure on the two was byte-identical, so the tier bought company features and not one minute of extra runner. Business now leases 8192 MB and 4 CPUs for 240 minutes (reclaimed after 30 idle minutes) against Business Lite's 4096 MB, 2 CPUs and 120 minutes, and TestBusinessRunnerLimitsExceedBusinessLite asserts a strict inequality on every resource key so the two cannot converge again unnoticed. The lease stays under runnersessions.MaxSessionMinutes (480), which is the ceiling a bad limits value is clamped to.

max_upload_mb (issue #364) joins the catalogue as a resource limit: how big one attached file may be, per workspace, resolved through the same layers. It is the one limit an upload handler needs BEFORE it knows which workspace the request belongs to — parsing a multipart body spools its parts to disk — so orgs.MaxPlanUploadMB derives a request ceiling from the capped plans rather than a second number being written down beside the first. The uncapped plans are skipped rather than collapsing the answer to "no bound": a plan with no ceiling means OpenV rations nothing, not that one HTTP request may be any size.

One ceiling sits outside those layers. A personal workspace seats one person, applied after the operator's own setting, because it describes what a personal workspace is rather than rationing it. The domain already refuses members and invitations there, more specifically than a seat count can and with the status the API spec documents, so the seat check stands aside and the limit exists to be reported rather than to enforce. The limits response marks it fixed, and the panel draws a fixed ceiling in grey instead of the red it paints a full workspace.

Every count limit goes through one check, so that no ceiling, the off-by-one and the refusal wording cannot drift apart between handlers. A refusal is 403 with the limit key, the amount used, the amount allowed and a remedy chosen from the deployment mode: an upgrade for a hosted member, the setting to change for a self-hoster, and a shared workspace for somebody adding a person to their personal one. A per-file upload refusal is a 413 instead, because the request is what is too large rather than the workspace being full. A limit whose usage cannot be counted is never enforced, so a database fault cannot turn into a billing message.

artifacts.title: Workspace limits resolve, report and refuse correctly
artifacts.body:
Preconditions: a deployment with a shared workspace and the tester's personal workspace, and shell access to set the deployment's environment.

1. With no OPENV_LIMITS set, open Settings → Limits on the shared workspace. Every count limit reads "No limit". Add a member and create a project; neither is refused.
2. Set OPENV_LIMITS to {"max_members": 2, "max_projects": 2} and restart. The panel now reads 1 of 2 members. Invite a second person without accepting the invitation: the panel reads 2 of 2, showing that an unaccepted invitation holds its seat.
3. Invite a third person. The call is refused with 403 and the body names max_members, allowed 2, used 2, and a remedy offering a plan upgrade. The existing member, the pending invitation and every project are still there afterwards.
4. Set OPENV_LIMITS to {"max_membrs": 2} and restart. The server refuses to start and names the unknown key.
5. Restore a valid OPENV_LIMITS, set OPENV_SELF_HOSTED=true and restart. The refusal in step 3 now names OPENV_LIMITS instead of offering an upgrade, and a workspace created before the setting was applied is no longer capped by its stored plan.
6. Open Settings → Limits on the personal workspace, with the deployment-wide max_members of 50 still in force. Workspace members reads 1 of 1, is marked as a ceiling nothing raises, is drawn without the colour a full workspace gets, and its description says to create a shared workspace.
7. Add a person to the personal workspace by both POST /orgs/{id}/members and POST /orgs/{id}/invitations. Both are refused with 400, and the message tells the tester to create a shared workspace rather than to upgrade a plan or change a setting. Repeat with OPENV_SELF_HOSTED unset: the answer is the same.
8. Set the personal workspace's own limits column to {"max_members": 0}, which would mean no ceiling anywhere else. The panel still reads 1 of 1 and step 7 still refuses.
9. Put one workspace on the business_lite plan and another on business, with no OPENV_LIMITS and no stored limits. Open Settings → Limits on each. Every resource limit on the Business workspace reads higher than the same limit on the Business Lite one — runner memory, CPUs, lease, idle window, evidence storage and largest figure — so the tier that contains the other grants more than it (issue #361). The unit test TestBusinessRunnerLimitsExceedBusinessLite asserts the same inequality against the plan defaults.
10. On each of those workspaces, read Settings → Limits for *Largest figure*, then attach a file just under that number and one just over it. The first is stored; the second is refused with 413, and the message names that workspace's own ceiling rather than a deployment-wide one (issue #364).

Pass: every step behaves as described, and no existing member, project or file is removed at any point.

artifacts.title: Baseline capture, authorship and large responses
artifacts.body: The system shall record which account captured each baseline. The system shall show that account's name wherever a person chooses between baselines. The system shall keep a baseline and its snapshot after an administrator deletes the account that captured it. The system shall report no author for a baseline that no account captured. The system shall compress a response when the client accepts compression and the response exceeds the configured floor. The system shall send an event stream uncompressed and unbuffered, whatever the client accepts. The system shall tell a reader that a baseline is loading until its snapshot arrives. The system shall show the live project when a baseline fails to load, and shall state why. The system shall state a reason whenever it refuses to capture a baseline.

artifacts.title: Content-type-driven compression and attributed baselines
artifacts.body:
Compression is one middleware wrapping the finished response, so it sees whatever any layer below produced. It decides on the first write rather than up front, because the decision depends on the Content-Type the handler set, and that is not known until the handler has run.

Two exclusions carry the weight. An event stream is never compressed: the API holds those connections open for minutes, and a compressor batches output until its window fills, so compressing a stream does not slow it down, it stops it — silently, until somebody notices their notifications never arrive. Reading the handler's own Content-Type rather than matching a list of paths means a stream added later is protected without anybody remembering to register it, and a handler that flushes before any type is known is treated as a stream too. Responses below a small floor are also left alone, because the gzip header and trailer cost more than they save. The wrapper implements http.Flusher so streaming handlers keep working, and drops any Content-Length the handler computed, which describes the uncompressed body and would truncate the response if it survived.

A baseline records the account that captured it. The column is nullable and the foreign key sets it null when the account goes, because a baseline is what a later argument about what was agreed is settled against and must outlive the people in the project; a baseline nobody can be attributed to is reported as having no author rather than as one whose name failed to load. The name is resolved with a left join on read, so no client ever renders an identifier.

The snapshot itself stays one document. Both places a person picks a baseline are native select elements, so the name, the date and the author share a single line of option text. While the snapshot is in flight the reader is told it is loading, because the view switches to the baseline the moment the picker changes and would otherwise draw an empty project; a failed load returns to the live project rather than leaving that emptiness on screen.

artifacts.title: Baselines carry their author and load without appearing broken
artifacts.body:
Preconditions: a project holding enough requirements that its export is at least 100 KB, and two accounts with editor access.

1. As the first account, capture a baseline. Open the baseline picker: the entry shows the baseline's name, its date and that account's name.
2. Request the baseline list over the API with Accept-Encoding: identity, then with Accept-Encoding: gzip. The second response carries Content-Encoding: gzip and Vary: Accept-Encoding; the first carries neither. Decompress the second and compare it to the first: they are identical byte for byte.
3. Request the baseline detail the same two ways. The compressed response is several times smaller and decompresses to exactly the uncompressed one.
4. Open an event stream, such as the notifications stream, offering gzip. The response carries no Content-Encoding, and its first keepalive arrives as readable text rather than as compressed bytes, while the connection stays open.
5. Select the baseline in the requirements view. Until its snapshot arrives the view says it is loading; it never shows an empty project.
6. Select a baseline that cannot be loaded, for example by deleting it from another session first. The view reports why and returns to the live project rather than showing an empty baseline.
7. Delete the account that captured the baseline. The baseline is still listed, still opens, and now shows no author rather than a missing name or an identifier.
8. Capture a baseline through an automation holding a workspace key rather than a signed-in account. It is listed with no author, and nothing in the interface claims one.
9. Trigger the capture action with no project open. The interface states why nothing was captured instead of doing nothing at all.

Pass: every step behaves as described, and no baseline is lost or altered at any point.

artifacts.title: Attachment catalogue, kind-aware serving, and the one viewer
artifacts.body:
How a figure stopped meaning "an image" without splitting the numbering or loosening what the platform will render.

**One catalogue, keyed by extension.** `internal/domain/attachments/kind.go` names every format the platform accepts and what it will do with it. The key is the file extension rather than the declared type because a browser sends `application/octet-stream` for nearly every CAD format; a declared image type is still honoured for a file whose name says nothing, since that is the case where the browser does know. A format may carry a signature (`%PDF-`, `ISO-10303-21`, `PK`, `glTF`), and one without a dependable signature — binary STL, the vendor part formats — is accepted on its extension. Nothing rests on that check: it catches a mis-named file, not a hostile one.

**Kind, derived not stored.** `KindForMime` maps a recorded type to image, document, model or other, and `MarshalJSON` puts it on every attachment and version, so no migration was needed and it cannot drift from the MIME type. `image/vnd.dxf` and `image/vnd.dwg` are deliberately models: their registered types begin `image/` and nothing can draw them. Every reader that used to assume an attachment was an image now asks `IsImage`.

**Serving is an allowlist of one.** Only a raster image is `Content-Disposition: inline`. SVG, PDF, CAD and anything else go out as downloads under `sandbox; default-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'`, and the API-wide `X-Frame-Options: DENY` is left standing. That is what makes storing an opaque or scriptable file safe, and it is why the relaxation a framed PDF preview would have needed was not made.

**Previewing without conceding any of that.** The application fetches the bytes with the member's session and renders them on its own origin: a PDF through a blob URL retyped to `application/pdf`, an STL parsed and drawn by `StlPreview` — a painter's-algorithm canvas renderer, no 3D library, ~60k triangles before it samples and says so. Every other model format gets a panel naming it and a download, because STEP and the native formats need a geometry kernel and an approximation of a part is worse than none: a reviewer would trust it.

**What the widening would have broken.** An attachment with a figure ref was categorised as a figure whatever its format, so a datasheet would have been packed under "figures" in a download and run through the report's image embedder, printing "is not an image the document can embed" mid-specification. `AttachmentCategory` now requires an image, with a `models` group added, and the report loads only image figures while still indexing every figure so a citation of one resolves.

The image sniffer was left image-only rather than widened: avatars and workspace logos share it and must stay pictures. `uploadLooksLikeFigure` dispatches instead.

artifacts.title: Attachment catalogue and viewer suite
artifacts.body:
Go suite over the catalogue and the serving policy (`internal/domain/attachments/kind_test.go`, `internal/api/attachment_safety_test.go`), plus the client helpers and the model reader (`frontend/src/components/attachmentKinds.test.ts`, `frontend/src/components/StlPreview.test.ts`).

1. Accepting an upload: the extension decides the recorded type for a CAD file the browser could not name, a PDF is accepted whether or not the browser named it, a wrong declared type does not beat the extension, a declared image type is honoured for a file with no extension, and a charset on the declared type is ignored.
2. Refusing: an executable, an HTML file, a zip, a file with no extension and an unnamed type, and an empty name are all refused.
3. Kind: every accepted type maps to image, document, model or other; a DXF and a DWG are models despite their `image/` types, so nothing tries to embed one.
4. Signatures: a real PDF and a real STEP file pass, a mis-named one of each is refused, a binary STL and a vendor part file pass on their extension, and an empty file never passes.
5. JSON: every attachment and every version carries its kind, and the rest of the record survives the added field.
6. Stored names keep the extension a download needs: `.pdf`, `.step`, `.stl`, `.sldprt` all survive into `REQ-17-FIG-3.<ext>`.
7. Serving: only a raster image is inline; SVG, PDF, every model type and an unspecified byte stream are downloads. A non-picture is served under a sandbox that permits nothing and refuses framing, with sniffing off; a picture keeps the policy that lets it render as one.
8. The image sniffer stays image-only — it refuses a PDF, which the avatar and logo uploads depend on — while the figure sniffer accepts the catalogue, refuses a mis-named PDF, and refuses a PDF presented as a PNG, which would be served inline.
9. Client: a CAD file the browser typed as a byte stream is accepted before sending and an unsupported one is not; a format is named by what it is rather than by its extension; an STL is recognised by type or by name; a file size reads as a person would say it.
10. The STL reader: binary and ASCII both parse, the facet normal is recomputed rather than trusted, the bounding box is measured, an ASCII file opening with "solid" is not misread as binary, a non-STL is refused, and a mesh over the drawing budget is sampled and reports that it was.

Pass: every assertion holds.

artifacts.title: Ref matching in the search predicate, gated by release channel
artifacts.body:
How REQ-161 is built.

**Normalising the query.** `artifacts.NormalizeRef` (`internal/domain/artifacts/ref.go`) trims and upper-cases what was typed and runs it through `ParseRef`, returning the canonical ref or "" when the text does not name one. `SearchInProjects` trims the query once at the top so the ILIKE pattern, the ref comparison and the snippet all read the same text — the API handler trims too, but the service is reachable from callers that do not.

**Matching and ranking.** `SearchInProjects` (`internal/persistence/postgres/artifact_repository.go`) adds `ref ILIKE $2` to the predicate and `(ref = $4) DESC` to the head of the ORDER BY, so an exact ref outranks a title match, a longer ref containing the query, and a body that cites it. The ref predicate has no trigram index but is served by the unique `(project_id, ref)` index for the exact case, and is cheap regardless: refs are short and few. The hit carries `COALESCE(ref, '')` back in `SearchHit.Ref`.

**Mode routing.** `GlobalSearch` (`internal/api/search_handlers.go`) dispatches a query that normalises to a ref onto the keyword path whatever mode was requested: an identifier is an address, and nearest-neighbour ranking has nothing to say about one. A ref-shaped phrase that matches no ref (`ISO-9001`) routes there too, which is lossless — the keyword path matches titles and bodies as well.

**The gate.** `release.FeatureSearchByRef` ("search-by-ref", shipped in 0.10.0). The handler resolves it once per request and passes `artifacts.SearchOptions{MatchRefs: …}` down through every mode, since hybrid runs the keyword path too. With it off the SQL is built without the ref predicate, without the ref ranking term and without the fourth bind parameter — postgres rejects a bind supplying one the statement does not use — and `SearchHit.Ref` is cleared, so an ungated workspace gets exactly the title/body search it had before. The UI reads the same key through `useFeature` for the placeholder wording; the ref badge needs no separate gate, because the server only sends a ref when the feature is on.

**Agents.** The MCP `search_artifacts` tool filters client-side over `/api/v1/artifacts`; it matches refs and hoists an exact one to the front by the same rule. It is not channel-gated, matching the existing policy that a request with no member session sees every feature.

artifacts.title: History tab: one feed, filtered on the auto-entry flag
artifacts.body:
How REQ-162 is built.

**The feed was already both things.** `chatter.ChatterEntry` carries `IsAutoEntry` and an `EntryType` — "comment" for what a member wrote, and "version-change", "status-change", "link-change", "figure-change", "restore", "test-result" or "guided-flow" for what the system recorded. The tab was called Comments while showing all of them, so the rename to History corrects the label rather than changing what is shown.

**The filter is that same flag.** `ChatterPanel.tsx` holds a `HistoryFilter` of 'all' | 'changes' | 'comments' and derives `visibleEntries` in a `useMemo`: 'changes' keeps `is_auto_entry === true`, 'comments' keeps `false`. Filtering is client-side because the feed is loaded whole for one artifact — switching filters is instant and costs no request, and there is no pagination whose page size a server-side filter would have to respect. No API or schema change.

**The control** is the shared `ui/SegmentedControl`, which already wraps its options rather than clipping them on a narrow panel.

**Empty is a normal state now.** The panel previously rendered nothing when there were no entries, which was survivable while the list was everything and rarely empty. A filter makes empty ordinary, so `EMPTY_HISTORY` names what each filter would have shown.

**One trap worth closing.** Posting a comment while reading 'changes' would file it where its author cannot see it, which reads as the button having failed. `handleAddMessage` moves the filter back to 'all' in that one case.

Not gated on a release feature key: the rename must not leave two labels in the product, and the filter narrows what the tab already displayed rather than reaching anything new.

artifacts.title: Artifact history tab and filter suite
artifacts.body:
Automated. Verifies REQ-162.

`frontend/src/components/ChatterPanel.history.test.tsx`. Fixtures: one recorded change ("Version 2 saved", is_auto_entry true) and one comment ("Checked against the datasheet", false).

1. The tab is labelled History.
2. The default view shows the change and the comment together.
3. **Changes** shows the recorded change and hides the comment.
4. **Comments** shows the comment and hides the recorded change.
5. Filtering to **Comments** with only changes present says "No comments yet" rather than rendering an empty panel.
6. An artifact with no entries at all says "Nothing yet".
7. A comment written while reading **Changes** is visible afterwards — the filter returns to **All** rather than swallowing it.

Confirmed load-bearing by mutation: making the filter a no-op failed 3 and 4; blanking the empty-state text failed 5 and 6; removing the filter reset alone failed 7 with the other cases still passing.

artifacts.title: Note tagging: two markers, one menu, and handles that match the server
artifacts.body:
How REQ-163 is built, and the change it makes to REQ-52.

**The handle problem, first.** `@name` mentions already resolved server-side (`internal/domain/mentions`), but nothing offered the handles, so people typed them from memory — and an unmatched `@token` is indistinguishable from prose, so a mention that named nobody looked exactly like one that worked. `noteMentions.ts` mirrors `mentions.Handles` exactly (name without spaces, first name, email local part) and writes **the first handle the server's `@([\w.-]+)` pattern can capture whole**. A name like "Ciara O'Brien" produces `ciarao'brien` first, which that pattern stops at, so the first name is written instead; a member with nothing capturable is left out of the menu rather than offered and silently dropped.

Those two lists must agree. `TestHandlesOrderMatchesTheComposer` pins the Go side to the same table the TypeScript tests use, so changing one without the other fails a test instead of shipping mentions that name nobody.

**`@@` raises the to-do.** `todoTargets` resolves the doubled markers against the members, and `ChatterPanel.raiseTodosFor` calls `createNoteTodo` — extracted from `AddTodoControl` so the shortcut and the after-the-fact button produce the same card. It runs **after** the note is saved and never rolls it back: the note is what the writer came to do, so a board that refuses the card is reported rather than allowed to swallow the comment. The existing control is unchanged and still the way to set a title, a person and a due date.

**One menu, two vocabularies.** `ui/TokenMenu` is the dropdown, extracted from `ArtifactEditor` so the composer and the description editor offer the same thing in the same shape. `activeMentionQuery` mirrors `activeReferenceQuery` down to the word-boundary and three-or-more rules, so `@` behaves like `#` and someone who has learnt one has learnt the other. Only one menu opens at a time: the caret is inside at most one token.

**Composer context is lazy.** Members, project artifacts, the artifact's links and the project's attachments are fetched on the first trigger keystroke, not when the panel opens — most notes are prose, and nobody should pay four requests for a menu they never summon. A failed fetch leaves the menus empty rather than breaking the composer, because the tokens can still be typed by hand.

**Notes stay plain text.** `NoteText` splits a note on the tokens it knows and leaves every other character as typed. Running years of existing notes through a markdown renderer would start reinterpreting every asterisk and leading hash people have already written, so the note body is not markdown and this does not make it markdown.

**The REQ-52 change.** `##` used to offer figures alone, on the reasoning that an artifact citation without a traceability link is a claim the matrix cannot see. It now offers every artifact too. The concern was real and is now carried by the marker rather than by refusing the citation: a single `#` is still the narrow, link-backed menu, and `##` says in the text as well as the menu that the citation reaches outside those links. People were writing those references by hand anyway, where nothing marked them at all.

**Gate.** `release.FeatureNoteTagging` ("note-tagging", 0.11.0) covers the composer menus and the `@@` shortcut as one thing — a workspace either has tagging in its notes or it does not. Rendering is never gated: a note already written with `@@dana` or `##REQ-12` shows its tags for everybody.

artifacts.title: Unlinked citation lint suite
artifacts.body:
Automated. Verifies REQ-164.

`internal/domain/quality/unlinked_citation_test.go`, 11 cases:

1. A citation to an unlinked artifact is one finding, at **error** severity, matching the citation as written and naming the artifact.
2. The same citation with the link present raises nothing.
3. A single-hash citation is flagged too — the link can be deleted after the text is written, which is exactly when the check earns its keep.
4. A figure citation raises nothing, under either marker.
5. An artifact citing its own ref raises nothing.
6. A text naming one artifact three times reports it once.
7. With `Context{}` — links never read — the rule stays silent, so "we did not look" cannot read as "nothing is linked" and flag every citation in the project.
8. A markdown heading, `PR#12` and `ISO-9001` raise nothing.
9. The rule can be switched off through the project's rule set.
10. `LinkedRefsByArtifact` counts links in both directions and does not connect two artifacts that only share a neighbour.
11. `LintProject` judges citations against the export's link graph, so the project report and the single-artifact endpoint agree.

The helper filters to this rule alone, so an unrelated wording finding on a fixture cannot make a case pass.

Mutation-checked: dropping the `LinksKnown` guard failed case 7; dropping the figure skip failed case 4. Both were reverted and re-run green.

artifacts.title: Upload ceiling across the proxy, and upload duration and progress
artifacts.body:
Covers the clauses of REQ-93 that no in-process test reaches: the ceiling a proxy in front of the API applies, the absence of a client-side time limit, and progress reporting. TC-49 covers BodyLimitMiddleware and the handlers' own MaxBytesReader; neither sees the nginx hop nor the browser's own clock, which is how a 32 MB proxy cap and a 60 s axios timeout both went unnoticed while the in-process tests stayed green.

**Client has no time limit on an upload** — automated, `frontend/src/api/client.upload.test.ts`. Each multipart call (attachment upload, new figure version, evidence file) sends `timeout: 0` rather than inheriting the instance's 60 s JSON timeout. Confirmed to be a live guard: restoring the inherited timeout fails three of the eight assertions.

**Progress is reported while the file is in flight** — automated, same suite. `onUploadProgress` maps to a whole percentage, rounds a fraction, clamps above 100, and reports null while the body's length is unknown; no handler is registered when no caller asked for progress.

**A proxy in front of the API refuses nothing the endpoint allows** — manual, and the gap worth noting. `client_max_body_size 0` on the nginx `/api/` location is not exercised by any automated check: the frontend suite never starts nginx, and the API suite is in-process and never sees it. Verify against a deployed environment by posting a body larger than 32 MB and confirming the API answers (401 unauthenticated, or the workspace's own 413 naming its number) rather than a bare nginx 413. The pre-fix measurement on production was a 33 MB body refused in 0.75 s after 8 MB sent, against a 1 KB body reaching the app and answering 401.

Re-run the manual step after any change to frontend/nginx.conf or to the plan upload ceilings in internal/domain/orgs/limits.go.

artifacts.title: As a maintainer, I need staging's database to hold production-shaped data, anonymised, so that a migration that backfills existing rows is proven on staging rather than first on production.
artifacts.body: Rationale: Discovered while amending REQ-141 (staging environment). Staging starts empty and fills only with what smoke runs create, which exercises a schema migration but not a data migration: BackfillOrgs and PromoteOrgColumns, and any future data-shaped migration, run against a nearly empty table there. The gap is not closable by the staging environment itself — it needs a periodic anonymised restore of a Railway Postgres backup, and no anonymisation tooling exists (internal/seeds seeds defaults only; scripts/backup.sh is compose-only and does not apply on Railway). Recorded as a candidate rather than folded into REQ-141, whose amendment deliberately guarantees the weaker but achievable "no data copied from production".

artifacts.title: Personal spaces
artifacts.body: Every user shall automatically receive a personal workspace on registration.

artifacts.title: Company workspaces
artifacts.body: Companies shall have workspaces with admin and member roles, and named teams of users.

artifacts.title: Per-project access grants
artifacts.body: Project access shall be grantable per user and/or per team, with role levels (owner, editor, viewer); a member's effective role is the highest of their direct and team grants.

artifacts.title: Authentication
artifacts.body: The system shall support email and password session authentication, Google sign-in, and sign-in through a generic OpenID Connect provider an operator configures. The system shall bind an account to the first identity provider it signs in with and shall refuse a later sign-in for the same email through a different provider. The system shall hash passwords with bcrypt and shall refuse a password shorter than eight characters.

artifacts.title: Workspace deletion
artifacts.body: A workspace admin shall be able to delete a company workspace. Deletion hides and locks the workspace immediately for all members; its projects and data are retained and restorable by a workspace admin for 30 days, after which the workspace and all contained data are permanently deleted by a scheduled purge. Personal workspaces cannot be deleted.

artifacts.title: Workspace AI budget and usage
artifacts.body: The system shall let a workspace admin set a monthly AI spend budget for the workspace and shall show each workspace its month-to-date usage. The system shall notify the workspace admins once when usage reaches 80 percent of the budget and once more when it reaches 100 percent, at most once per threshold per month. When an operator enables budget enforcement, the system shall refuse to launch a new run in a workspace that has exhausted its budget; otherwise the system shall warn only.

artifacts.title: Plan limits
artifacts.body: Each workspace shall carry a plan whose defaults bound the resources a runner may use: hosted runner memory and CPU, transient lease lifetime and idle window, and the first-refusal grace window. A workspace shall be able to override an individual limit, and the system shall fall back to the plan default for any override that is missing or not a number, so that a corrupt setting never yields an unbounded limit.

artifacts.title: Workspace invitations by email
artifacts.body: A workspace admin shall be able to invite an email address to a company workspace at a chosen role. The system shall keep one pending invitation per address and workspace. The system shall carry an invitation as a one-time link and shall store the link's token hashed. An invitation link shall expire 7 days after issue. The system shall mail the link when the operator has configured a mailer, and shall show the link to the admin in every case. An invitation shall convert to membership only when the acting account proves control of the invited address. The system shall accept registration with the link and the invited address as proof. The system shall accept a signed-in account whose address equals the invited address presenting the link as proof. The system shall accept a sign-in through a provider that asserts the address as verified as proof. The system shall never change the role of an existing member through an invitation. A workspace admin shall be able to list and revoke pending invitations. The system shall throttle invitation creation per inviting account. The system shall refuse invitations to a personal workspace.

artifacts.title: Project share links
artifacts.body: A project owner shall be able to mint a share link of one of two kinds: a public link, which shall open the live project read only to anyone holding it without an account, and a reviewer link, which shall grant the reviewer role to the signed-in account that takes it up. Each link shall carry a label and an optional expiry, shall be revocable, and shall be stored as a hash of its token, which the system shall show once at creation and never again. The system shall answer every unusable link (unknown, revoked or expired) with one identical not-found response and shall throttle link lookups per address. A share link, when pasted into a service that unfurls links, shall present a preview card naming the project and its workspace, served by the platform itself.

artifacts.title: Reviewer role
artifacts.body: The project role ladder shall include a reviewer role ranked between viewer and editor. A reviewer shall be able to read everything a viewer reads and to add notes, comments and mentions, and the system shall refuse a reviewer every write that changes an artifact, a link, a status, a baseline or a project setting. The role shall be grantable by name and to a team like the other roles, and a reviewer share link shall grant it without lowering a stronger role the account already holds.

artifacts.title: Workspace plan set by a platform admin
artifacts.body: The system shall let a platform admin move a workspace to another plan through the API, accepting only the plan names the platform defines and refusing the request from any account that is not a platform admin. On a plan change the system shall keep the workspace's release-channel override and shall resolve the effective channel from the new plan's default where no override is set.

artifacts.title: Platform admin page and admin standing
artifacts.body: The system shall provide platform admins with a page, reachable from the account menu, that lists every workspace on the deployment with its type, plan and member count and lets the admin change a workspace's plan in place, and that lists every account with its platform-admin standing and lets the admin grant or remove that standing. The system shall refuse a platform admin's request to remove their own standing and any request that would leave the deployment with no platform admin, and shall refuse every request on these endpoints from an account that is not a platform admin.

artifacts.title: Default workspace at sign-in
artifacts.body: The system shall let a member choose the workspace their sign-in lands in, from the workspaces they belong to. The system shall land a member who has chosen none in their personal workspace. The system shall store the choice against the member's own account and shall accept a change only from that member. The system shall refuse a choice naming a workspace the member does not belong to, with the same answer as for a workspace that does not exist. The system shall treat the personal workspace as the absence of a choice. The system shall check the member's membership of the chosen workspace on every sign-in. The system shall land a member whose chosen workspace they have since left in their personal workspace. The system shall clear the choice when the chosen workspace is purged. A workspace switch made during a session shall take precedence over the choice for that session. A tab reloaded during a session shall stay in the workspace it was in. The choice shall be a gated feature that reaches a stable-channel workspace with its next stable release.

artifacts.title: Entitlement resolved from the billed plan and the billing status
artifacts.body:
The system shall record the billed plan of each workspace. The system shall record the billing status of each workspace. The system shall resolve every workspace limit from the billed plan while the billing status is none, trialing, active or past due. The system shall resolve every workspace limit from the free tier's plan while the billing status holds any other value. The system shall apply the workspace's own limit settings above the plan whatever the billing status holds. The system shall apply the deployment's limit settings above the plan whatever the billing status holds. The system shall keep a workspace on its billed plan while the billing status is past due. The system shall refuse to move a workspace onto a granted plan while the workspace holds a live subscription. The system shall report the billed plan, the entitled plan and the billing status to any member of the workspace. The system shall report no billing provider identifier to any member.

The system shall resolve a flag limit through the same three layers as a numeric limit. The system shall read an absent flag as allowed.

artifacts.title: Billing inert without a provider
artifacts.body: The system shall start no billing job when the operator configures no billing provider. The system shall make no request to a billing provider when the operator configures none. The system shall answer every billing route with a not-found response when the operator configures no billing provider. The system shall keep billing off on a deployment the operator configures as self-hosted, whatever billing configuration the deployment holds. The system shall log that it kept billing off on such a deployment. The system shall resolve every limit of a workspace with no billing relationship exactly as it does with no billing provider. The system shall refuse to start when the billing price map fails to parse. The system shall start when the billing provider does not answer.

artifacts.title: Scheduled reconciliation with the billing provider
artifacts.body: The system shall read every subscription from the billing provider at start-up. The system shall read every subscription from the billing provider at a configured interval. The system shall apply each subscription's plan, status, interval, seat count and period end to the workspace that holds it. The system shall map a subscription to a plan only through the configured price map. The system shall refuse to start when the price map names a plan that the platform does not sell. The system shall leave a workspace's plan unchanged when a read from the billing provider fails. The system shall leave a workspace's plan unchanged when the subscription's price is absent from the price map. The system shall leave a workspace's plan unchanged when the subscription carries more than one item. The system shall leave a workspace's plan unchanged when it read the snapshot earlier than the snapshot the workspace already holds. The system shall attach each subscription to one workspace or to none. The system shall attach a subscription to a workspace only through the workspace's stored subscription reference or the workspace identifier the subscription carries. The system shall cancel a live subscription that belongs to no workspace. The system shall treat a subscription with an open payment dispute as lapsed until the dispute closes. The system shall keep a workspace on a granted plan whatever subscription the workspace holds. The system shall report the age of the oldest applied snapshot as a metric. The system shall re-read one workspace's subscription on an administrator's request. The system shall leave the workspace unchanged when that read fails.

artifacts.title: Self-service subscription from workspace settings
artifacts.body:
The platform shall let a workspace admin start a subscription to the Business Lite plan or the Business plan from the Billing tab in workspace settings.

The platform shall offer each plan monthly and yearly, in GBP, USD and EUR.

The platform shall take payment on the billing provider's hosted checkout page, so that no card detail reaches the platform.

The platform shall verify that a completed checkout session names the workspace before it records the subscription.

The platform shall record the subscription before the Billing tab renders after the return from checkout.

The platform shall refuse a checkout for a workspace on a plan a platform admin granted.

The platform shall refuse the Business plan for a personal workspace.

Rationale: the paid layer is the company layer; the product itself stays free. A hosted checkout keeps the platform out of card-data scope.

artifacts.title: Plan change and billing management for a subscribed workspace
artifacts.body:
The platform shall let a workspace admin move a live subscription to another plan or interval in place, keeping one subscription per workspace.

The platform shall bill the Business Lite plan at a quantity of one.

The platform shall bill the Business plan at the workspace's seat count.

The platform shall open the billing provider's self-service portal for the payment card, the billing address, the tax id, the receipt email, invoices and cancellation at period end.

The platform shall show a workspace that already holds a subscription its Billing tab on every release channel.

Rationale: the provider prorates a change only within one subscription; product switching stays out of the portal so the seat quantity always follows a plan change.

artifacts.title: One trial per buyer and one live subscription per workspace
artifacts.body:
The platform shall attach a 14-day trial to a checkout only while the buyer has never used a trial.

The platform shall mark the buyer's trial used when it records the subscription.

The platform shall key the trial on the person, not the workspace.

The platform shall refuse a checkout while the workspace holds a live subscription.

The platform shall cancel the newer subscription when a second completed checkout binds to a workspace that already holds a live one.

The platform shall fix the workspace's currency at its first purchase.

Rationale: a person can create workspaces freely, each its own billing customer, so a trial keyed on the workspace is a free tier with extra steps.

artifacts.title: Billed seats follow the workspace's members
artifacts.body:
The platform shall set a Business subscription's billed quantity to the workspace's members plus pending invitations within one reconcile interval of a membership change.

The platform shall commit a membership change before it contacts the billing provider.

The platform shall complete a membership change when the billing provider fails.

The platform shall coalesce every membership change queued within one two-second drain into one quantity push per workspace.

The platform shall repair a billed quantity that differs from the seat count on every reconcile tick.

The platform shall refuse to push a quantity above the configured seat ceiling and shall count the refusal.

The platform shall never change a Business Lite subscription's quantity.

Rationale: the member count leads and the provider follows; an under-billed hour costs less than a runaway invitation loop's invoice.

artifacts.title: Plan flags enforced at the gated action
artifacts.body:
The platform shall refuse a hosted worker's run claim for a workspace whose plan does not include hosted automation.

The platform shall accept a claim of the same run by the member's own Agent Connector whatever the plan.

The platform shall refuse creating a hosted runner for a workspace whose plan does not include hosted automation.

The platform shall refuse creating a people-team, and granting a team on a project, for a workspace whose plan does not include teams.

The platform shall refuse the workspace usage rollup and the workspace budget for a workspace whose plan does not include the workspace budget.

The platform shall answer each flag refusal with the code limit_reached and the flag's name.

Rationale: a gate belongs where the gated thing happens, so a cron automation claimed by the member's own machine is never refused.

artifacts.title: Monthly cloud-runner minutes allowance and alerts
artifacts.body:
The platform shall count a workspace's leased cloud-runner minutes per calendar month from its runner sessions, a live session measured to now.

The platform shall shorten a cloud-runner lease to the minutes left in the month's allowance.

The platform shall refuse a cloud-runner lease once the month's leased minutes reach the allowance.

The platform shall never count a run on a member's own machine through the Agent Connector.

The platform shall notify the workspace's admins once when the month's leased minutes reach 80% of the allowance and once more at 100%.

The platform shall show the month's leased minutes beside the allowance on the Limits tab.

artifacts.title: Observability
artifacts.body: The system shall expose an unauthenticated liveness endpoint, a Prometheus metrics endpoint that an operator can gate with a bearer token, and a structured request log that names the resolved workspace, user and actor kind on every line. Metrics shall be labelled by route template, method and status only, never by project, user or agent, so that cardinality stays bounded. The system shall record HTTP request counts and latency, run lifecycle counts and gauges, and live stream connection counts.

artifacts.title: Backup and restore
artifacts.body: The self-hosted stack shall produce one timestamped backup bundle holding a database dump, the data volume and the uploads volume, on demand and on a configurable schedule, shall write a bundle under a temporary name and rename it only on success, and shall prune bundles older than a configurable retention. The stack shall restore any such bundle. On a managed platform the operator documentation shall state which of those three stores the platform's own backups cover and which the operator must back up separately.

artifacts.title: Forward-only schema migration
artifacts.body: The system shall advance the database through a numbered migration ledger at startup, applying each migration exactly once inside its own transaction together with its ledger row, under a database lock so that concurrent instances never apply a migration twice. A failed migration shall leave neither the schema change nor its ledger row behind. The system shall never edit an applied migration.

artifacts.title: Define products without a team
artifacts.body: As a solo founder I need to define one or more products and manage their complete requirement sets on my own, so that I can run a real product process without hiring.

artifacts.title: Guided requirements definition
artifacts.body: I need step-by-step, conversational guidance that turns rough product ideas into structured requirements, because I am not a requirements engineer.

artifacts.title: AI does real work under my control
artifacts.body: I need AI agents to perform meaningful requirements and development work, while every change they make passes through my explicit approval.

artifacts.title: Bring my own AI
artifacts.body: I need to use the Claude, GPT or Gemini subscription I already pay for, and my company needs its own metered API-token AI - not platform-marked-up inference.

artifacts.title: One view of human and AI work
artifacts.body: I need a single board that shows what both my human colleagues and my AI agents are working on, so nothing falls between the two.

artifacts.title: Company workspaces and access control
artifacts.body: My company needs private workspaces with admins, teams and per-project access so different groups can work without seeing each other's data.

artifacts.title: Audit-ready traceability
artifacts.body: I need end-to-end traceability from stakeholder needs through requirements to verification evidence, so the product can face audits and regulated customers.

artifacts.title: Capture stakeholder input effortlessly
artifacts.body: I need to gather requirements from internal and external people who will never open a requirements tool - a link they can click and just talk.

artifacts.title: Predictable agent execution
artifacts.body: I need agent work to start reliably regardless of which colleague is online, while runs I launch still prefer my own machine and subscription first.

artifacts.title: Nothing runs without my consent
artifacts.body: I need certainty that OpenV runs nothing in the background on my machine: a runner executes only while I have deliberately opened it, and stops when I close it.

artifacts.title: Demo material I did not have to invent
artifacts.body: As someone trying, demoing or testing OpenV I need a supply of believable throwaway products to drive the wizard with, so that I never have to spend a real product idea or type a fake one to see the tool work. Because that material now comes from other people, I also need whatever reaches my screen and my agent's context to be inert, attributable and removable.

artifacts.title: Run it myself without an operations team
artifacts.body: As a solo founder or company admin I need to run OpenV on my own host or on a managed platform, keep its data safe, see that it is healthy, and know that the parts exposed to the internet are hardened, because I have no operations or security team to do that for me.

artifacts.title: Act on my product from my phone
artifacts.body: As a founder, admin or contributor away from my desk I need to approve or reject what my agents and colleagues propose, read the requirement someone linked, answer a comment or ask the assistant, move a board card, and start a cloud runner and sign an agent in, all from my phone or tablet, because the work does not wait for me to be at a desktop and nothing should need installing.

artifacts.title: Know the cost and the way out before I commit
artifacts.body: As a prospective user evaluating OpenV, I need to learn what it does, what the hosted service costs, what self-hosting involves and how my data leaves if I stop, all before I create an account, so that adopting it is a decision I can defend to my team and reverse without loss.

artifacts.title: Choose when changes reach my workspace
artifacts.body: I need to decide when a new release reaches my team's workspace, so an update never lands in the middle of an audit, a product release of our own, or a training session, while security fixes still reach us at once and I can see and try what is coming before it arrives.

artifacts.title: Flow requirements down to subsystems and suppliers
artifacts.body: I need to break a large product into subsystem and supplier projects that each carry their own requirements, keep every one of those traced to the requirement it refines above it, see verification flow back up so I know the top-level requirement is met, and hand a supplier exactly its share of the requirements without exposing the rest.

artifacts.title: Show the project to people who are not on the team
artifacts.body: As a project owner, I need to hand a customer, an assessor or an outside reviewer the project itself, read only or with the right to comment, without making them a member or sending them a file that goes stale, so that review happens on the live specification and the decision to let somebody edit stays mine.

artifacts.title: SEC-1 Prompt injection into auto-approving vendor CLIs
artifacts.body: Severity: High. Affects: self-hosted and Railway. Runners start Gemini with --approval-mode auto_edit (internal/runner/geminicli.go:112) and Codex with --sandbox workspace-write and no tool allowlist (codexcli.go:140); Claude Code receives an allowlist only when the agent defines one (claudecode.go:158). Untrusted text reaches those prompts: the public interview transcript is concatenated into the interviewer prompt (internal/api/suite_handlers.go:1528) and that agent holds the OpenV tools; repository-access agents run inside a real checkout; the V&V Assistant fetches web pages. An external participant, a repository file or a web page can therefore carry instructions the CLI acts on with auto-approved edits or commands, and proposal gating protects OpenV data only, not the runner host or its credentials. Recommendation: REQ-91.

artifacts.title: SEC-2 Hosted runner containers lack isolation hardening
artifacts.body: Severity: Medium. Affects: self-hosted only (hosted runners are off on Railway). internal/hosting/docker.go:84-115 sets memory and CPU caps but no capability drop, no no-new-privileges, no read-only root, no pids limit and no dedicated network; provider API keys enter as container environment; the API itself holds the host's Docker socket when the feature is enabled (docker-compose.yml). Combined with SEC-1 a compromised agent reaches the host and long-lived keys. Recommendation: REQ-96.

artifacts.title: SEC-3 Tenant-chosen api_key_env reads any runner host variable
artifacts.body: Severity: Medium. Affects: both. Provider settings validate provider and auth mode but not the api_key_env name (internal/domain/providers/providers.go:66,160-181); the worker reads os.Getenv on that name and injects the value into the agent's environment (internal/runner/worker.go:368). A workspace admin can name WORKER_API_KEY, RUNNER_POOL_KEY, DATABASE_URL or any other host variable, and an agent (SEC-1) can then read it. Recommendation: REQ-92.

artifacts.title: SEC-4 Weak development defaults in the base compose stack
artifacts.body: Severity: Medium. Affects: self-hosted only. docker-compose.yml runs Postgres with password "postgres" and publishes port 5432 on the host, and defaults WORKER_API_KEY to "dev-worker-key"; the backup sidecar falls back to the same password. The production overlay correctly makes these required and unpublishes the port, so the exposure is a deployment that runs the base file on a reachable host. Recommendation: REQ-97.

artifacts.title: SEC-5 No throttling on sign-in, registration or run launch
artifacts.body: Severity: Medium. Affects: both; confirmed live on production 2026-09-06 (eight failed sign-ins in under two seconds all answered 401 with no back-off).
