Rate limiting exists only on the public interview endpoints (internal/api/handlers.go:233-235). bcrypt slows guessing but nothing locks or throttles an account or an address, and the limiter is in-memory and single-instance. Recommendation: REQ-90.

artifacts.title: SEC-6 SVG attachments served inline with uploader-supplied type; no body size limit
artifacts.body: Severity: Medium. Affects: both. image/svg+xml is an accepted image type (internal/api/handlers.go:2335), the client-supplied MIME type is stored, and downloads are served with Content-Disposition inline (handlers.go:2275), so an SVG carrying script executes on the API origin for a viewer who opens the download URL directly. Uploads are read with io.ReadAll and no MaxBytesReader, and a 2 MB JSON body to the sign-in endpoint was accepted on production. Mitigated by viewer authentication on download and the SPA rendering images through img tags only. Recommendation: REQ-93.

artifacts.title: SEC-7 Known-vulnerable docker/docker module compiled into the API
artifacts.body: Severity: Medium self-hosted, Low on Railway. govulncheck reports GO-2026-4887 and GO-2026-4883 in github.com/docker/docker v28.5.2 (no fixed version yet), reachable through internal/hosting/docker.go, plus six advisories in required-but-not-called modules. Railway runs with HOSTED_RUNNERS=off so the code path is dormant there. Recommendation: bump when a fix ships; REQ-98.

artifacts.title: SEC-8 Frontend production dependency advisory (fast-uri)
artifacts.body: Severity: Low. Affects: both. npm audit --omit=dev reports one high advisory in fast-uri 3.0.0-3.1.5, a transitive build-time dependency with little runtime exposure in the static bundle. Recommendation: bump the override pin; REQ-98.

artifacts.title: SEC-9 Live invite tokens written to the request log
artifacts.body: Severity: Low. Affects: both. The request log records the URL path (internal/api/requestlog.go:62) and the public interview routes carry the raw invite token in the path, so anyone with log or proxy access holds a live token until it expires. Tokens themselves are strong (32 random bytes, stored as SHA-256). Recommendation: REQ-97.

artifacts.title: SEC-10 API image runs as root
artifacts.body: Severity: Low. Affects: both. Dockerfile.api has no USER directive, so the API process runs as root inside its container; the frontend (USER nginx) and worker (USER worker) images already drop privileges. Recommendation: REQ-97.

artifacts.title: SEC-11 No browser security headers reach production; CSP permissive by design
artifacts.body: Severity: Medium on Railway, Low self-hosted. frontend/nginx.conf declares X-Frame-Options, nosniff, Referrer-Policy and a CSP at server level, but every location block adds its own add_header (caching), and nginx drops inherited add_header directives in any location that sets one. Confirmed live on 2026-09-06: the production frontend and its static assets return none of those headers, and the API returns no HSTS, nosniff or frame header on any response. The declared CSP is also permissive (unsafe-inline, unsafe-eval, any http/https origin). Recommendation: REQ-94.

artifacts.title: SEC-12 Backups unencrypted and on-host by default
artifacts.body: Severity: Low. Affects: self-hosted only. scripts/backup.sh writes a plain tar.gz holding a full pg_dump (accounts, bcrypt hashes, hashed tokens, every tenant's data) plus both volumes to ./backups on the host, with no encryption and no off-host copy. Recommendation: support encrypting bundles and pushing them off-host; REQ-88 documents the managed-platform split.

artifacts.title: SEC-13 CORS reflects any origin with credentials when configured as wildcard
artifacts.body: Severity: Low. Affects: both, only when misconfigured. cmd/server/main.go:636-640 reflects the caller's Origin and sets Allow-Credentials true whenever CORS_ORIGIN is "*". Production is configured with the exact frontend origin and a foreign origin received no CORS headers on 2026-09-06, so this is a latent footgun rather than a live exposure. Recommendation: REQ-100.

artifacts.title: SEC-14 Production metrics endpoint is open
artifacts.body: Severity: Low. Affects: Railway production (configuration). GET /metrics on openv-production.up.railway.app returned 61 KB of Prometheus output to an unauthenticated client on 2026-09-06: Go runtime statistics, request counts and latency per route template, run lifecycle gauges. Nothing tenant-specific leaks, but it maps the API surface and its load for anyone. The gate exists (OPENV_METRICS_TOKEN) and is simply not set on the Railway service. Recommendation: set OPENV_METRICS_TOKEN on the OpenV service, or restrict the path at the edge.

artifacts.title: SEC-15 Open, unverified self-registration on production
artifacts.body: Severity: Medium on Railway, Low self-hosted. POST /api/v1/auth/register is open on production with no email verification, no invitation and no throttling (SEC-5). Anyone can create accounts and personal workspaces, read and report the shared demo-product pool, and consume database and storage; with a paired runner of their own they can also drive the agent surface. Whether that is intended for a public instance is a product decision, but there is no way to close it today. Recommendation: REQ-95.

artifacts.title: SEC-16 Sessions live 30 days with no idle expiry or password-change invalidation
artifacts.body: Severity: Low. Affects: both. users.SessionDuration is 30 days (internal/domain/users/users.go:25) with no idle timeout; sessions are invalidated on logout and swept on expiry, but nothing invalidates other sessions when a password changes. A stolen cookie is therefore usable for up to a month. Recommendation: REQ-99.

artifacts.title: Document model and rebuilt PDF and Word renderers
artifacts.body:
One document model feeds both documents. `internal/domain/reports/doc` parses each artifact body once with goldmark (GFM tables, task lists, strikethrough) into blocks — paragraphs, headings, ordered and bulleted lists, tables, code, quotes, rules — and inline runs carrying bold, italic, code, strikethrough, an external URL or a `#REQ-12` / `#REQ-12-FIG-1` citation, keeping the writer's soft line breaks as the editor does. `reports.buildReportModel` builds everything the renderers share: the tree in document order, section numbers, qualified titles, parsed bodies, figures decoded (PNG/JPEG kept, GIF/WebP/BMP/TIFF re-encoded to PNG, SVG and unreadable files as placeholder sentences), traceability rows deduplicated and sorted, field labels, and when asked for, coverage, gaps and the latest result per test case.

`pdf_report.go` (gofpdf with the Go TrueType family embedded as UTF-8): a cover with the workspace logo, the project, the boxed snapshot statement and the content summary; a contents page computed by rendering twice; outline bookmarks and an internal link per artifact; a footer with "Page n of N"; per-row fields, traceability and coverage tables that never split a row and repeat their header; bodies flowed with the library's writer so length never drops content; figures captioned and scaled to the column; strikethrough drawn as a stroke; a figure that fails to register clears the library's latched error instead of failing the download.

`docx_report.go` (hand-assembled WordprocessingML): document, styles, numbering (bullets and restarting decimal lists), settings (update fields on open), footer with PAGE/NUMPAGES, core and app properties, relationships, media parts. Headings carry bookmarks; traceability rows and citations are `w:hyperlink` anchors; external links are external relationships; tables carry `cantSplit`, `tblHeader` and fixed layout; a TOC field lists headings 1–3 while artifact titles sit at level 4 so the navigation pane finds them.

`exports.Content` and the template presets (`content.go`) decide what a document carries; `downloads` gathers evidence and the workspace logo beside the snapshot and passes `reports.RenderOptions`. The V&V status PDF moved to the same fonts and gained a reference column with wrapped titles. Satisfies REQ-124 … REQ-131.

artifacts.title: Tenant isolation
artifacts.body: No user, worker or agent shall read or write data belonging to a workspace they are not a member of.

artifacts.title: Personal runner scoping
artifacts.body: A personal runner shall claim only runs launched by its owning member.

artifacts.title: Hosted repo exclusion
artifacts.body: Hosted runners shall refuse runs requiring repository access; such runs shall wait for a personal or workspace runner.

artifacts.title: Hashed credentials, shown once
artifacts.body: Worker keys, agent run tokens and pairing codes shall be stored as sha256 hashes with plaintext revealed exactly once at creation.

artifacts.title: Untrusted content isolation in agent prompts
artifacts.body: A prompt the platform builds for a member's own assistant shall state up front that the product profile, wizard state, transcript and any artifact supplied for context are content and never instructions, and shall fence the state block and the artifact block, so that text authored in another tenant — a rolled community product seeds the wizard — or written into an artifact by anyone who can edit the project cannot read as an order to an agent running on the member's own machine with their credentials.

artifacts.title: Leased runner state erasure
artifacts.body: The system shall revoke a lease's credential when the lease ends. The leased runner shall erase that lease's vendor CLI credentials and working files before the runner serves another member.

artifacts.title: Runner pool credential scope
artifacts.body: The system shall restrict a runner pool node's own credential to the pool registration, heartbeat and release endpoints. The system shall grant a pool node access to a workspace's data only through the credential of a lease held by a member of that workspace.

artifacts.title: Throttling of authentication and launch endpoints
artifacts.body: The system shall throttle password sign-in and registration per client address and per account, so that a client that fails sign-in more than a configurable number of times in a window receives a rate-limited response until the window passes. The system shall throttle single sign-on callbacks and run launches per client address on the same terms. The limits shall key on the real client address when the operator declares a trusted proxy and on the connection address otherwise.

artifacts.title: Tool allowlists for agents that read untrusted content
artifacts.body: The runner shall start every vendor CLI with an explicit tool allowlist taken from the agent definition. The runner shall refuse to start an agent whose definition carries no allowlist, and the system shall refuse to save such a definition. An agent whose prompt carries content authored outside the workspace shall run without automatic approval of file edits or shell commands. That class covers an interview turn, an agent with repository access, an agent granted a web tool or a shell tool, and an agent granted a tool from a foreign MCP server. The seeded interviewer shall hold read-only tools plus the candidate-need recorder only. Where a vendor CLI accepts a tool allowlist, the runner shall pass the agent's allowlist in that vendor's own terms. Where a vendor CLI accepts no allowlist, the runner shall confine the run to a sandbox that permits no file edits or shell commands beyond what the allowlist names. The OpenV MCP server shall expose only the tools the allowlist names to every vendor CLI. The system shall refuse repository access for an agent on a vendor CLI that cannot confine edits per tool.

artifacts.title: Provider key environment names from a fixed catalog
artifacts.body: The system shall accept as a provider's key environment variable only a name from the platform's catalog for that provider, and shall reject any other name on write. The runner shall inject into an agent's environment only the variable the catalog names for the run's provider, so that a workspace setting can never cause a runner to read and expose an unrelated variable from its host.

artifacts.title: Upload limits and safe serving of attachments
artifacts.body:
The system shall cap the size of one uploaded attachment at a per-workspace limit. The system shall resolve that limit through the same layers as every other workspace limit. The system shall name the workspace's own ceiling when it refuses a larger file. The system shall stop reading an oversized upload before it has read the whole of it. The system shall store no file when it refuses an upload.

The system shall cap every request body that carries no uploaded file at an operator-configurable limit. The system shall let each upload endpoint set the ceiling for its own request. The general body cap shall never lower the ceiling an upload endpoint sets. The system shall apply no request-body ceiling at a proxy in front of the API that is lower than the ceiling the upload endpoint sets. The system shall read no more of an uploaded file into memory than the format check requires.

The system shall bound an upload by the size of the file rather than by the time the file takes to send. The system shall apply no client-side time limit that aborts an upload still in progress. The system shall report the progress of an upload while the file is in flight.

The system shall serve every attachment with a content type sniffed from its bytes rather than the one the uploader supplied. The system shall serve an SVG, and any other script-capable format, as a download rather than inline. The system shall send a no-sniff header and a sandboxing content security policy on every attachment response.

artifacts.title: Browser security headers
artifacts.body: Every response from the API and from the frontend server shall carry a no-sniff header, a frame-denying header, and a referrer policy. Every response served over TLS shall carry a strict transport security header. The frontend shall carry a content security policy that permits scripts from its own origin only, without unsafe inline or unsafe eval, and that names the API origin as the only connect source. The frontend server configuration shall apply these headers on every location, including those that set their own caching headers.

artifacts.title: Registration policy
artifacts.body: An operator shall be able to close self-service registration, so that new accounts arrive only through an invitation from a workspace admin or through the configured single sign-on provider. While registration is open the system shall throttle it per client address. The system shall document, for each deployment option, whether registration is open.

artifacts.title: Hosted runner container hardening
artifacts.body: The hosted runner provisioner shall create each container with no new privileges, with every capability dropped, with a process count limit, and with memory and CPU caps, and shall attach it to a network that reaches the API and the provider endpoints only. The operator documentation shall state that mounting the host's container socket into the API grants the API control of the host, and shall present the transient runner pool as the alternative that needs no socket.

artifacts.title: Secrets absent from logs and default configuration
artifacts.body: The request log shall redact the token segment of a public interview or connector path so that a live token never reaches a log line. The API shall refuse to start with the development worker key or the development database password when it listens on a non-loopback address. The base compose file shall not publish the database port to the host. The API image shall run as a non-root user.

artifacts.title: Session lifetime and idle expiry
artifacts.body: A session shall expire after an operator-configurable absolute lifetime. A session shall expire after an operator-configurable idle period. The default absolute lifetime and its ceiling shall be 30 days, and the default idle period and its ceiling shall be 7 days. A member shall be able to change the account password from personal settings by presenting the current password and a new one of at least the minimum length. When a password changes, the system shall invalidate every other session of the account and keep the session that made the change.

artifacts.title: Cross-origin policy refuses wildcard with credentials
artifacts.body: The API shall allow credentialed cross-origin requests from the single configured frontend origin only, and shall refuse to start when the configured origin is a wildcard, so that no deployment can reflect an arbitrary origin together with credentials.

artifacts.title: Dependency vulnerability scanning in CI
artifacts.body: The continuous integration pipeline shall run a Go vulnerability check over the server and worker binaries and an audit of the frontend's production dependencies on every pull request, and shall fail the run on a reachable vulnerability of high severity or above.

artifacts.title: Email verification for password sign-ups
artifacts.body: On a deployment with an outbound mailer configured, the system shall email a single-use verification link to each new password account. The link shall stay valid for 24 hours. Until the account follows the link, the system shall refuse every API request from its browser session outside the authentication routes with a 403 response that carries the code email_unverified. During that time the system shall serve the account a verification page that offers to resend the link, to send it to a corrected address, and to sign out. The system shall change the account's address to a corrected one only after the account follows the link sent to that address. The system shall treat an account created through a single sign-on provider that asserts a verified address as verified. The system shall throttle resend and change requests per account. The operator shall be able to disable verification with OPENV_EMAIL_VERIFICATION=off. On a deployment with no mailer the system shall mark new accounts verified at sign-up. The system shall never apply the gate to worker keys, run tokens or the runner pool key.

artifacts.title: Password reset by emailed link or admin-minted link
artifacts.body:
The system shall let the holder of a single-use reset link set a new password for one password account. The system shall store only a hash of the link's token. The system shall refuse a link that is unknown, spent or expired with one answer that does not say which.

On a deployment with a mailer configured, the sign-in page shall offer a reset by email. The system shall answer a reset request for any well-formed address with the same status. The system shall do the lookup and the send after answering, so that neither the answer nor its timing reveals whether the address has an account. The system shall send the link only to the account's own address. An emailed link shall expire one hour after the system issues it. The system shall throttle reset requests per client address and per address asked for, whether or not that address has an account. On a deployment with no mailer the system shall tell the requester to ask the administrator instead.

A platform admin shall be able to mint a reset link for any password account and shall receive the link once. The system shall not email an admin-minted link. An admin-minted link shall expire 24 hours after the system issues it. The system shall log each admin-minted link with the admin's and the account's ids.

Setting a password through a link shall check the password rule before spending the link. Setting the password shall end every session of the account. Following an emailed link shall mark the account's address verified; following an admin-minted link shall not. The system shall refuse to mint a link for an account that signs in through an identity provider.

artifacts.title: MCP stdio tool server
artifacts.body:
Hand-rolled JSON-RPC MCP server (31 tools as of 2026-09-18) is the only data path between agents and OpenV: requirements, links, V&V evidence, coverage and gaps, baselines, kanban, proposals, quality rules, the project map and context bundles. Runs over stdio beside the agent CLI, authenticating with the run token agentd injects, or - for sessions that are not a platform-launched run, such as an agent maintaining this project - a workspace runner key from the environment. Enforces the lean-context rule by construction.

`confirm_link` clears the suspect flag on one link (`PUT /api/v1/links/{id}/confirm`, the same call the link panel makes), so an agent that has re-read both ends of a trace can answer the question the flag asks instead of handing it to someone with a browser. `list_links_for_artifact` reports the flag, which is how the waiting ones are found. The API's refusal stands unchanged: a proposal-mode run is refused outright rather than diverted to a proposal, because clearing suspect asserts that a human re-read the trace and routing that through a proposal would defeat the review the flag exists to trigger (REQ-66).

Read-only classification is a property of the table, not of the handler: `readOnlyTools` names every tool an agent held to reading may have, and a tool absent from it is treated as a writer, so a tool added later grants nothing until someone lists it deliberately. Writers are named for what they change, and a test pins that convention against the read-only set so a misclassification fails rather than silently widening the least-privilege grant.

artifacts.title: Server-side proposal diversion
artifacts.body: Write endpoints detect an agent run context and divert mutations into proposal records; approval replays the operation as the reviewing human.

artifacts.title: agent_runs queue with routing claims
artifacts.body: The agent_runs table is the job queue (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED). Claim SQL scopes personal keys to their owner's runs and holds reserved runs until hosted_after expires.

artifacts.title: agentd host worker with CLI adapters
artifacts.body: agentd polls for runs and drives claude/codex/gemini CLIs with openv-mcp wired in; interactive vendor sign-in is brokered to a visible console on the member's machine.

artifacts.title: Hosted runner provisioner and token-mode image
artifacts.body: Docker provisioner creates one openv-worker container per workspace; provider keys enter as container env at provision only; the image runs CLIs headless in API-key mode and claims with repo-access excluded.

artifacts.title: OpenV Agent Connector
artifacts.body: openv-connector:// protocol app: self-registers per-user, exchanges one-time pairing codes for the member's personal runner key, and starts agentd in its own console window. No service registration of any kind.

artifacts.title: Workspace authorization ladder
artifacts.body: Request authorization resolves platform admin, org admin, direct and team project grants, run-own-project and worker-same-org in one ladder; workers carry org and optional user scope from their key.

artifacts.title: Crew builder UIs
artifacts.body: Cytoscape-based org-chart editor with department containers and hierarchical layout, plus a network-diagram editor with typed edges; both edit the same crew graph.

artifacts.title: Shared products service and cross-tenant tables
artifacts.body: internal/domain/sharedproducts plus migration 0021 (shared_products, shared_product_reports). Sanitize-on-write flattens every field to inert single-line text; publication is gated to session principals, deduplicated by normalized name, and bounded by a per-workspace daily limit and a global pool ceiling, both env-tunable (OPENV_SHARED_PRODUCT_DAILY_LIMIT, OPENV_SHARED_PRODUCT_POOL_LIMIT). Distinct-reporter counting hides an entry at three. Neither table carries a foreign key to organizations: community content outlives the workspace that published it, and a workspace purge must not retract other people's roll list.

artifacts.title: artifacts.SectionNumbers document-order numbering
artifacts.body: A pure function over a project's live artifacts that walks the tree in document order (sort order, then creation time, then ID, so equal sort orders still number deterministically) and issues hierarchical numbers to headings only. A dangling parent is treated as a root and a parent cycle terminates, so a broken tree still numbers. The list handler exposes it behind doc_numbers=1 and reads the whole project to serve it, because a page or a type filter is a slice through the tree and cannot be numbered on its own.

artifacts.title: Invention quality gate
artifacts.body: describeProductFlaws enforces the invariants the built-in concepts already meet — the name riffs on the gimmick rather than bolting a suffix onto an unrelated product, the vision carries the name, the description is one mechanism in the 'A <what> that <what it does>.' shape, the audience is a qualified clause rather than a demographic, and the problem never names the product — phrased in the words the retry quotes back to the agent. A weak reply buys one retry; anything still below the bar is kept locally but never published.

artifacts.title: Remote MCP transport
artifacts.body: Proposed, not built: an HTTP MCP transport placed in front of the existing exported tool table, so the remote endpoint and the stdio server run the same handlers and no second tool implementation appears. Member-level authorization and per-client consent replace the bearer credential the stdio server takes from its environment.

artifacts.title: Layered quality rule sets
artifacts.body: A settings JSONB column on organizations and projects holds a rule set under one key, resolved defaults → workspace → project so each level stores only its own diff. The linter keeps one pattern set per convention and takes the resolved set as an argument, so it stays pure and a report can carry the rules that produced it. Unknown conventions, rules and severities are dropped on read and refused on write, and a settings read failure degrades to the platform defaults rather than failing the report. Agents receive the same resolved set through the tool surface and as a House style line in the AI map header.

artifacts.title: Server-side event name resolution
artifacts.body: The events endpoint decorates each stored event with an actor kind, the identifier inside the actor string and the display names behind it, plus the kind and name of the affected entity. Resolution runs only over the events that survive the project-visibility filter, so no identifier the caller may not see is ever dereferenced. Names come from the payload the publishing handler stamped in where it has one and from a repository lookup otherwise, memoized per page so a repeated actor, agent or artifact costs a single query. Every lookup is nil-safe and failure-tolerant: an unresolvable name is omitted and the client falls back to the raw identifier it still receives.

artifacts.title: Runner pool and lease protocol
artifacts.body: Pre-warmed agentd processes register against a deployment-wide pool key and heartbeat; a lease atomically reserves one idle node (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) and mints a session-scoped personal runner key handed to the node once, on the heartbeat that picks the lease up. A server-side sweep ends lapsed leases (hard expiry, idle window, lost node) and revokes their keys. Needs no Docker daemon at the API, so it runs on platforms that offer replicas but no docker socket.

artifacts.title: Headless CLI sign-in relay
artifacts.body:
A leased runner has no console and no browser, so each vendor flow is relayed through the existing login broker: TUI sign-ins (claude setup-token) run over a pseudo-terminal with a wide window so the URL does not soft-wrap, and the pasted code is typed back into it; loopback sign-ins (codex) have their redirect pasted back and replayed against the CLI's own advertised local port, using only the pasted path and query so another host cannot be reached.

Gemini is a paste-back flow (`NO_BROWSER=1`) that also has to name its authentication mode. The CLI refuses to start non-interactively unless one is named — it prints "Please set an Auth method in your ~/.gemini/settings.json ..." and exits 41 — and a lease's fresh HOME holds no settings file that could have named it. `geminiOAuthEnv` (`GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_GCA=true`) names Google-account OAuth on the sign-in command, and `geminiRunEnv` names the same mode for a headless run, which is the mode the credentials a sign-in leaves under ~/.gemini belong to. The environment is the lever rather than the run's isolated settings file because the CLI reads the member's own `security.auth.selectedAuthType` first and falls back to the environment only when that is unset. `geminiAuthNamed` withholds the variable from any run whose own or inherited environment already names a mode (an API key, Vertex, a gateway base URL), since `GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_GCA` outranks all of them in the CLI's resolver and would otherwise move the run onto another account.

The tier wall is told BEFORE the flow, not only after it (issue #360). Since 18 June 2026 Google serves Gemini CLI only to accounts on a Gemini Code Assist Standard or Enterprise licence; the free, Google One, AI Pro and AI Ultra tiers moved to Antigravity CLI, so Code Assist OAuth from one of those lands on Google's deprecation page after everything on this side has worked. `geminiTierNote` already appended that explanation to a failed sign-in, which is a warning arriving after the wall. `providerCautions.tsx` now carries the same statement as a `caution` on ProviderConnectCard, rendered above the Connect button on both the user settings panel and the workspace providers tab, and it names the remedy that is still served: a workspace Gemini API key, which is also what the Antigravity CLI agent runs on. The caution is keyed by provider so the mechanism generalises to the next vendor that withdraws a sign-in, and it hides itself once a sign-in is in flight, where the flow's own wording is what matters.

artifacts.title: Browser hardening headers on API and frontend
artifacts.body: internal/api/security_headers.go stamps X-Content-Type-Options nosniff, X-Frame-Options DENY, Referrer-Policy strict-origin-when-cross-origin and a default-src 'none' content security policy on every API response, plus Strict-Transport-Security when SECURE_COOKIES or CROSS_SITE_COOKIES declares a TLS-only deployment. The frontend's headers live in frontend/security-headers.conf, included in the nginx server block and again in every location that adds its own header, because nginx discards inherited add_header directives there. The frontend CSP permits scripts from the app's origin only (CRA's runtime chunk is built as a file with INLINE_RUNTIME_CHUNK=false and the theme bootstrap is public/theme-init.js), style-src 'self' plus inline styles for React, images from self, data, blob and the API origin, and connect-src self plus the API origin; the Docker build substitutes REACT_APP_API_URL into the policy and runs nginx -t so a broken configuration fails the image build.

artifacts.title: Credential endpoint throttling
artifacts.body: The token-bucket limiter already guarding the public interview routes (internal/api/ratelimit.go) now also guards the credential endpoints. Sign-in charges every attempt against the client address (OPENV_AUTH_IP_BURST 30, 120 per hour) and only a failed attempt against the normalised account email (OPENV_AUTH_ACCOUNT_BURST 5, 20 per hour), using a check-then-penalize pair so a correct password never spends the account's budget; registration charges per address (5, 10 per hour); the Google and OIDC start and callback routes charge per address (20, 60 per hour). A throttled request is answered 429 with Retry-After. Buckets are in-memory and per API instance, keyed on the real client address only when OPENV_TRUST_PROXY=1. Run launches are not yet throttled.

artifacts.title: Provider key variable catalog
artifacts.body: providers.AllowedAPIKeyEnvs fixes the environment variable names a provider setting may carry as api_key_env to ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY and GOOGLE_API_KEY, or blank for the provider's default. providers.Upsert refuses any other name with ErrInvalidSetting (a 400 at the API), and the runner (internal/runner/worker.go) independently refuses to start a run whose claim names a variable outside the catalog, failing the run with a configuration error, so a row written before the rule or a hostile API cannot turn a runner into a reader of its host's secrets.

artifacts.title: Request caps, upload sniffing and sandboxed SVG downloads
artifacts.body:
How big one uploaded figure may be is the workspace limit `max_upload_mb` (orgs.LimitMaxUploadMB), resolved through the same three layers as every other limit. Plan defaults: free 128 MB, Business Lite 512 MB, Business 1024 MB, self-host and enterprise uncapped. `OPENV_MAX_UPLOAD_MB` still wins where an operator set it, so a deployment that pinned the old 25 MB keeps it. The refusal is a 413 naming the workspace's own number rather than saying only that the file is too large. The 25 MB the platform shipped with was chosen when a figure meant a screenshot; once the catalogue accepted CAD it made a mid-sized assembly unattachable, so the catalogue advertised formats the uploader refused (issue #364).

api.BodyLimitMiddleware wraps every request body in http.MaxBytesReader at OPENV_MAX_BODY_MB (32 MB) EXCEPT a multipart/form-data request, which it leaves alone. Nesting one MaxBytesReader inside another enforces the tighter of the two, so the API-wide number silently overrode whatever an upload handler asked for: the figure cap could not be raised past it, and UploadEvidenceFile's own 200 MB cap had never been reachable. Each multipart handler now bounds its own request before parsing — UploadAttachment at a deployment ceiling derived from orgs.MaxPlanUploadMB (the form has to be parsed before the artifact, and therefore the workspace, is known), UploadAttachmentVersion at the workspace's own limit, UploadEvidenceFile, UploadAvatar and UploadOrgLogo at theirs.

The in-process middleware was not the only cap in front of the handlers. The frontend image serves the API same-origin — nginx proxies `/api/` to it (frontend/nginx.conf), and the built bundle carries no absolute API origin — and that location set `client_max_body_size 32m` to mirror OPENV_MAX_BODY_MB. Exempting multipart inside the process did nothing about the hop in front of it: nginx went on answering anything over 32 MB with a 413 of its own, before the API saw the request, so the plan ceilings stayed unreachable and #364's fix was masked at the edge. Measured against production: a 33 MB body was refused in 0.75 s after 8 MB, a small one reached the app. The directive is now `client_max_body_size 0`, delegating to the API rather than naming a bigger number — a ceiling written at the proxy is a second copy of a limit that lives in the plan table, and the first copy went stale the moment the table changed. Nothing is unbounded as a result: JSON routes are still held by BodyLimitMiddleware, each multipart handler by its own MaxBytesReader, and `proxy_request_buffering off` means nginx streams the body to the API rather than spooling it.

The last cap was a clock rather than a size. The axios instance carries `timeout: 60000`, chosen for JSON calls, and axios counts its timeout as wall-clock across the whole request including the request body — so on an upload it was not a server deadline but a cap on how long the member's connection had to push the file, making the real ceiling their upstream bandwidth (about 7 MB at 1 Mbit/s, 37 MB at 5 Mbit/s). A file inside the workspace's plan failed with "timeout of 60000ms exceeded" and left no access-log line at all, because the browser aborted mid-body and the request never completed. Every multipart call now goes through a shared `uploadConfig()` carrying `timeout: 0`, leaving the refusal to the API's own per-workspace limit.

The frontend reads its guard from GET /orgs/{id}/limits (hooks/useUploadLimit.ts) rather than carrying a constant, cached per workspace; a failed lookup or an uncapped plan lets the upload proceed and leaves the refusal to the API, which is the only authority on it. `uploadConfig()` also takes an optional progress callback, mapping axios's onUploadProgress to a whole percentage and to null while the body's length is unknown: the figure gallery reports "Uploading... 42%" and the evidence uploader "Uploading… 2/3 42%". A large figure or evidence capture is minutes of uplink, and a control that says only "Uploading..." for that long is indistinguishable from a hung one — which is how the timeout presented before anyone traced it.

artifacts.title: CORS wildcard refusal
artifacts.body: api.CORSMiddleware replaces the inline handler in cmd/server/main.go. It returns ErrCORSOriginNotAllowed for an empty, "*" or "null" CORS_ORIGIN and the server refuses to start, so no deployment can reflect an arbitrary Origin together with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials. A matching origin receives the credentialed allow headers and Vary: Origin; any other origin receives none and a foreign preflight is answered 200 without them.

artifacts.title: Request-log token redaction
artifacts.body: RequestLogMiddleware logs redactPath(r.URL.Path): for any path under /api/v1/public/interviews/ the invite-token segment is replaced with [token] before the line is written, so a live invite never reaches the access log or whatever aggregates it. Other paths are logged unchanged. Covers the log half of REQ-97; the development-default refusal and non-root API image remain open.

artifacts.title: Same-origin API proxy in the frontend image
artifacts.body: Built (PR #299, Phase 0 of the mobile plan) and live in production since 2026-09-07 19:55 UTC (release 4be9bd4). The frontend's nginx proxies `^~ /api/` to the API. The upstream address (`API_UPSTREAM`: the API service's Railway private domain on port 8080, or `api:8080` in compose) and the container's nameservers are written into `/etc/nginx/openv/api-proxy.conf` at container start by `frontend/docker-entrypoint.d/40-openv-api-proxy.sh`; the upstream is proxied through a variable so nginx re-resolves the name through DNS on every request instead of pinning a private address that changes on each API redeploy. Server-sent events and downloads stream unbuffered with a one-hour read timeout; `client_max_body_size 32m` matches the API's body cap; X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Proto (from the edge when present) and Host are forwarded; the location adds no frontend security headers because the API sets its own. Production builds leave `REACT_APP_API_URL` empty and the client defaults to a relative `/api` on its own origin; the content security policy's connect-src and img-src collapse to 'self'. The session cookie is then a first-party `SameSite=Lax` cookie, `CROSS_SITE_COOKIES` comes off, and CORS is never exercised. For the remaining split deployments the API sets the `Partitioned` attribute on the session and OIDC cookies whenever `CROSS_SITE_COOKIES` is on. The 27 MB connector download goes through the proxy unbuffered, so it needed no special case. Verified locally with a real nginx against a fake upstream: routing (including `^~` precedence over the asset regex for paths such as `/api/v1/attachments/x.png`), forwarded headers, unbuffered streaming, and a 413 above 32 MB. Production switch, applied in this order so sign-in kept working throughout: frontend service `API_UPSTREAM=openv.railway.internal:8080` with `REACT_APP_API_URL` emptied (rebuild), then API service `CROSS_SITE_COOKIES=false` and `PUBLIC_URL` on the frontend origin (redeploy). Verified live afterwards: the frontend's `/api/v1/auth/config` answers 200 through the proxy, the index CSP is `connect-src 'self'`, the bundle carries no API domain, a workspace runner key authenticates through the proxy, proxied responses carry the API's HSTS, nosniff, DENY and CSP headers, and the API's own domain still serves connectors directly.

artifacts.title: Responsive shell: viewport classes, drawer navigation and stacked panes
artifacts.body:
Built (PR #299, Phase 1 of the mobile plan). `frontend/src/hooks/viewport.ts` defines two breakpoints, phone (width ≤ 640 px) and tablet (≤ 900 px), and `useViewport` reports the class, `isPhone`, `isCompact` (phone or tablet) and `coarsePointer` (the `(hover: none) and (pointer: coarse)` media query), kept current across resizes and orientation changes. Components that change shape read it once: ProjectLayout renders a top bar with a 48 px menu button below the tablet breakpoint and the navigation as a drawer over the page (closing on navigation, backdrop tap and Escape); on touch screens auto-hide panels behave as hidden and the edge strips widen to 24 px. ModuleView stacks into one pane at a time (Tree, Document, Notes) behind a segmented control; selecting an artifact moves to its document; panes are hidden rather than unmounted so tree state and editor drafts survive. GuidedWizard's StepShell replaces the 220 px rail with a progress strip and a native step picker; the V&V Assistant becomes a bottom sheet behind a floating button and stays mounted while closed. The manual (`/manual`) below the tablet breakpoint shows a top bar with a Contents button, the chapter title and an App link; its table of contents becomes a drawer over the page that closes on selection, backdrop tap or its close button, and markdown tables, code blocks and images scroll or shrink inside the chapter card. Global CSS: fields are 16 px on coarse pointers (no iOS focus zoom), the shell is 100dvh with a 100vh fallback, every table sits in an overflow-x wrapper, safe-area helpers and a reduced-motion rule; index.html declares viewport-fit=cover and the installed-app meta tags. Login, the create-workspace modal, the work-item drawer, the project-list navbar and the search popover no longer assume a desktop width; the help button moves into the top bar on phones. Verified by rendering the production build on Pixel 5 (Chromium) and iPhone 13 (WebKit) emulation with a mocked API, and by the mobile Playwright journey (TC-50).

Phone polish pass (2026-09-08, docs/plans/mobile-support.md §8). Dialog shells (`Modal`, `ConfirmDialog`, `PromptDialog`, the runner dialogs) share `ui/dialogCard.ts`: on a phone the card fills the width with 16 px padding and scrolls inside `100dvh`. Personal settings is a full-screen sheet whose Appearance and Notifications rows wrap, so the System / Light / Dark control is never clipped. `ui/SegmentedControl` and `ThemeSwitcher` wrap their options. `ui/Sheet.tsx` opens a side pane as a full-screen sheet below 900 px: the agent editor, a run's detail and a crew node's settings. The top bar on a phone is one row (logo, workspace switcher, bell, account) without the centred title; the workspace switcher's menu is fixed to the screen edges on phones. The runs, automations and V&V tables show only their identifying columns on a phone; the test-run and matrix grids pin a 150 px first column and hide the lowest-value columns. `index.css` gives touch screens a floor of 40 px for `.button`, `.button-secondary`, `.icon-btn`, selects and text fields, 36 px for every other button and 18 px for ticks; chips, refs, timestamps and tree glyphs are 12 px or larger. Product Overview, the agent editor, the version compare and the workspace details collapse to one column on a phone. The regression tool is `e2e/tools/phone-audit.js` (`npm run audit:phone`): it renders a served production build on a Pixel 5 against a mocked API, opens the sheets and dialogs reachable from 48 screens, and reports elements past the viewport, clipped containers, tap targets under 32 px, text under 12 px and page errors, with a screenshot per screen.

Desktop pass (2026-09-08, docs/plans/mobile-support.md §8, REQ-116). The audit tool gained ten desktop profiles (`npm run audit:desktop`): 1024×768, 1280×800, 1366×768, 1440×900, 1536×864, 1920×1080, 2560×1440, 3840×2160 at a device pixel ratio of 2 and HiDPI 1440 and 1920 at 2×; on a desktop profile it clicks instead of tapping, skips the phone-only drawer screens, applies a 24 px click floor and adds three wide-screen checks (text blocks over 900 px with over 200 characters, single-line fields over 720 px, rasters drawn above their pixel width). Findings and fixes: the requirements module at 1024 px drew the tree at its saved 400 px and the notes column at 320 px, leaving the document a 50 px sliver — `ModuleView` now draws the tree at its saved width clamped so the document keeps at least 420 px, and a first visit under 1200 px starts the notes column auto-hidden (a saved choice wins). Reading surfaces on a wide display share one token, `--measure: 1100px` (`theme.css`), through a `.measure` utility (`index.css`): the artifact document and its editor and the agent editor stop growing there and stay left-aligned with their pane; inside a measured surface a single-line field or its hint stops at `--measure-field` (720 px); tables keep their width and scroll. The baseline selector no longer takes the toolbar's full width (`width: auto`); workspace name fields and proposal review notes carry a maximum width. Click targets and text: the "Menu: Pinned" and "Notes: Pinned" mode buttons, the tree's move arrows, the test-run status select, the manual's heading links and the collapsed-panel strip glyph are at or above 24 px and 12 px. `desktop.spec.ts` (chromium, viewports from `test.use` at 1024×768 and 2560×1440) keeps the no-sideways-scroll, document-room and measure contracts under CI (TC-53).

artifacts.title: Touch parity: visible actions, Move to… dialog, pointer drag and board action sheet
artifacts.body: Built (PR #299, Phases 2 and 3 of the mobile plan; revised after the maintainer's first phone session). ArtifactList gives every row a visible ⋯ actions button that opens the same menu as right-click, positioned to stay on screen; the menu gains *Move to…*, a dialog that picks a target artifact from a native select in document order and a placement (before, after, inside), each option enabled only where `planMove` would accept the drop, and then calls the same reorder as a drop. Rows keep the HTML5 drag: mobile browsers start it from a long press on the row itself, so the grip handle that first shipped for coarse pointers was redundant and was removed. The row controls sit in one column in the order they act, Move up, More actions, Move down, and are 44 px on touch. KanbanBoard on phones shows one column at a time with previous/next buttons and a segmented column picker; each card's ⋯ opens an actions sheet with *Open card* and *Move to <column>*, which performs the same move as a drop (so a card moved to To Do launches its agent exactly as a drag would); a locked card (agent run in progress) keeps its moves disabled. ReviewQueue renders suspect links as cards with 44 px controls on phones. The notifications panel spans the screen below the top bar on phones. On phones the Requirements toolbar folds into an actions sheet behind one ⋯ button and the help panel opens from the shell's top bar. Muted text is raised to 4.6:1 contrast and the manifest gains shortcuts and categories.

artifacts.title: Landing view, public-path allowlist and single-sourced hosting copy
artifacts.body: Built (PR #302 merged as 6020854; four hosted tiers and the absolute Open Graph image in PR #303, merged as 5d720fe; tier renamed to Business Lite in a follow-up). `frontend/src/views/Landing.tsx` is a lazily loaded public view rendered at `/` when the startup session check finds no user (a signed-in user is redirected to `/projects`, and the app already withholds routes until that check settles, so there is no flash) and at `/pricing` scrolled to the pricing section. Its copy lives in `frontend/src/landing/content.ts` so the page, the unit test and the manual FAQ share one source: `HOSTED_TIERS` (Single User free; Business Lite, Business and Enterprise marked coming soon with `available: false`, no price, and a "Tell us you want this" issue link), `OTHER_TIERS` (Self-hosted and Charities, free forever), `ALPHA_NOTE`, the free-plan and team-plan runner limits mirrored from `internal/domain/orgs/limits.go`, the export formats from `downloadSelection.ts`, and the data-portability commitment. A `TierCard` renders each tier; the hosted row is four across on desktop, two on tablet and one on a phone via `useViewport`. `frontend/src/utils/publicPaths.ts` defines `isPublicPath` (exact `/`, and the `/login`, `/pricing`, `/manual`, `/interview` segments); the axios 401 interceptor uses it so no failed call can bounce a visitor off a public page. Login reads `?mode=register` to open registration directly and links back to the landing page. index.html carries title, description and absolute Open Graph tags; the hero and OG images are screenshots of the requirements module rendered from the production build against a mocked API. Issue templates `free-hosting` and `alpha-feedback` back the page's calls to action. No billing code: plan handling is out of scope.

artifacts.title: Sign-up email verification: policy, token table, middleware gate and wall
artifacts.body:
Policy: `notify.VerificationPolicyFromEnv(mailer)` returns `users.EmailVerificationPolicy{Required}` — true iff the SMTP mailer is enabled and `OPENV_EMAIL_VERIFICATION` is not `off`; one boot log line names the state. The policy reaches the user service (`Register` creates accounts verified when off, pending when on; `LoginWithSSO` always verified), the API handler and the auth middleware.

Data: migration 0024 adds `users.email_verified` (default FALSE) and `email_verified_at`, backfills SSO rows TRUE (the provider proved the address) and leaves password rows FALSE, and creates `email_verifications` (id, user_id, email, token_hash unique, expires_at, used, created_at) in the `connector_pairings` shape. `IssueEmailVerification(userID, email)` discards the user's unused links and stores a new SHA-256 hash with a 24 h expiry; `email` is the address the link went to. `ConsumeEmailVerification(hash, now)` spends the link with `UPDATE … WHERE NOT used AND expires_at > now RETURNING`, marks the user verified and applies the link's address in one transaction; a unique violation on the email index rolls back as `ErrEmailTaken`.

API (`internal/api/email_verification_handlers.go`): `POST /auth/verify-email {token}` (open) confirms; `POST /auth/verify-email/resend` and `/change {email}` read the session cookie themselves (the auth routes are open paths), refuse Bearer credentials, require `Content-Type: application/json` (forces a CORS preflight so a cross-site form cannot redirect a walled account's mail), and are throttled per account (`OPENV_VERIFY_RESEND_BURST` 3 / `_REFILL_PER_HOUR` 6). Register sends the link fire-and-forget; resend and change send synchronously with a 10 s bound (`notify.SendWithTimeout`) and answer 502 on failure. `/auth/config` reports `email_verification_required`. The mail is plain text through the existing `Mailer`; the link is `FRONTEND_URL/verify-email?token=…` (fallback `http://localhost:3000`).

Gate (`authmiddleware.go`): in the cookie branch, before the org is resolved, `policy.Required && !user.EmailVerified` answers `403 {"error":"email not verified","code":"email_unverified"}`; the open paths (`/health`, `/metrics`, `/api/v1/auth/*`, `/api/v1/public/*`) and every Bearer branch are untouched.

Frontend: `views/VerifyEmail.tsx` is the token landing (`?token=`) and the wall (resend with a 60 s cooldown, corrected address, "I've clicked the link", sign out, a 15 s poll of `/auth/me`); `App.tsx` reads `/auth/config` with `/auth/me`, and while `walled` replaces every protected route with a redirect to `/verify-email`; the axios interceptor sends a `403 email_unverified` there; `/verify-email` is a public path; `Login.tsx` lands an unverified account on the wall; the settings panel shows a Verified pill or a link to verify.

Rollout: the hosted instance has no SMTP, so migration 0024 marks every password account unverified but nothing is enforced; the operator adds `OPENV_SMTP_*` with `OPENV_EMAIL_VERIFICATION=off`, confirms delivery, then removes the switch (docs/railway.md, docs/operations.md, including the SQL to grandfather or unblock accounts).

artifacts.title: CI vulnerability gate and Moby client migration
artifacts.body:
Built (REQ-98; HAZ-7, HAZ-8). A `vuln` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs on every pull request and push to master beside the backend, frontend, docker and e2e jobs: `govulncheck` (pinned v1.8.0, installed under `GOTOOLCHAIN=auto` because the tool itself needs Go 1.26) over `./cmd/... ./internal/...`, which reports only vulnerabilities the binaries can reach, then `npm audit --omit=dev --audit-level=high` in `frontend/` for what ships to a browser. The frontend steps run even when the Go scan failed so one red scanner never hides the other. `make vuln` runs the same pair locally with the same exit semantics; `docs/DEVELOPMENT.md` documents the gate.

First run findings and their fixes: 29 standard-library advisories came from the stale `go 1.25.0` directive (the images already built with 1.25.14); the directive now matches. The frontend's `fast-uri` advisory (four GHSAs, high) is closed by an `overrides` entry to 3.1.7. The Docker client `github.com/docker/docker@v28.5.2+incompatible` carried GO-2026-4887 (CVSS 8.8) and GO-2026-4883 with no fixed release on that module path, so the hosted-runner provisioner (`internal/hosting/docker.go`) moved to `github.com/moby/moby/client` v0.6.0 with `github.com/moby/moby/api` v1.56.0; `github.com/docker/docker` is no longer a dependency. The port keeps the container, host and network configuration identical, now assembled by a pure `buildRunnerSpec` function with unit tests, and maps not-found through `containerd/errdefs`. The promote workflow requires every check on master to be green, so a reachable high-severity advisory now blocks a release until it is fixed.

artifacts.title: Mandatory allowlists, run trust, vendor translation and hardened runner containers
artifacts.body:
Built (REQ-91, REQ-96; HAZ-1, HAZ-2, HAZ-4, HAZ-10). `agents.Definition.Validate` refuses an empty `allowed_tools` (API 400, the editor blocks save) and refuses `repo_access` on any provider but claude-code; the worker refuses both before it clones anything, through the normal finish path as a non-retryable `agent_error`, and each adapter re-checks at `Start`. Existing definitions without a list are backfilled once from the seed that produced them (`seeds.SeedAllowedTools`, on both the database and the file-sync path, rewriting the file), locked agents excepted and logged.

Trust is a property of the run: `RunSpec.Untrusted` is true for an interview-origin run (`agentruns.Run.UntrustedOrigin`, carried in the claim) or for a definition that reaches outside (web tools, any shell grant, any foreign MCP server, repository access). Per provider: claude-code always runs `--permission-mode default` with `--allowedTools` as the whole approval surface; codex-cli runs `--sandbox workspace-write` only for a trusted run whose allowlist names a file or shell tool and `read-only` otherwise; gemini-cli gets the allowlist translated into `tools.core` and `mcpServers.openv.includeTools` (Claude tool names mapped to gemini built-ins, `Bash(git *)` and `Bash(git:*)` to `run_shell_command(git)`), with `--approval-mode auto_edit` trusted and `default` untrusted; no path passes a bypass flag. The OpenV MCP server itself filters its tool table through `OPENV_MCP_TOOLS`, which every adapter sets from the allowlist, so codex and gemini get real enforcement for the OpenV tools. The seeded interviewer holds the seventeen read-only OpenV tools plus `record_candidate_need`, narrowed on unedited installs by a seed version bump. Vendor limits that the CLI cannot enforce (`max_turns` on codex and gemini) are logged once per run rather than refused.

Hosted runner containers (`internal/hosting/docker.go`, on the moby client): `CapDrop ALL`, `no-new-privileges`, a pids limit (default 1024, `HOSTED_RUNNER_PIDS_LIMIT`), memory and CPU from the plan, only the org volume bound, the `RUNNER_NETWORK` when set; the root filesystem stays writable because the runner image's CLIs write caches outside `/data`. `docs/operations.md` states that mounting the host's container socket into the API grants the API control of the host and presents the transient runner pool as the socket-free alternative; `docker-compose.prod.yml` shows an `openv-runners` network only the API joins.

artifacts.title: Closeable registration, workspace invitations, session policy and password change
artifacts.body:
Built (REQ-95, REQ-99, REQ-117; HAZ-15, HAZ-16). Migration 0025 adds `org_invitations` (org, folded email, role, token hash, invited_by, expires_at, accepted_at, last_emailed_at; one pending row per org and address through a partial unique index that an upsert keeps the id across) and `sessions.last_seen_at`. `internal/domain/invitations` owns creation (personal workspaces refused, names joined in one query), lookup by hashed token, `FindPending`, and acceptance, which claims the row first, adds the membership second and un-stamps on failure; an existing membership is never re-roled. Acceptance paths: `POST /auth/register` with `invite_token` (address must match; the account is marked email-verified because the link proved the mailbox), `POST /auth/invitations/accept` for a signed-in account whose address matches (403 `invitation_email_mismatch` otherwise), and OIDC sign-in with a provider-verified address; the email-verification link grants no membership because the change-of-address flow could aim it at an invited address. `POST /auth/invitations/preview {token}` (own limiter) shows workspace, role and address to the link holder. `POST /orgs/{id}/members` and `/invitations` share one branch: existing verified account → 201 member, already a member → 409, unverified existing account or no account → 202 invitation with the link, mailed off the request path and stamped `last_emailed_at` on success; a delivered, unchanged invitation is not re-mailed within an hour. Invitation creation is throttled per inviting account (`OPENV_INVITE_BURST`, `OPENV_INVITE_REFILL_PER_HOUR`).

Registration policy `OPENV_REGISTRATION=open|closed` (default open, read at boot): closed answers 403 `registration_closed` unless the request carries a live invite token for the registering address; OIDC is unaffected; `GET /auth/policy` (public) reports the policy and `min_password_length`, and the Login view hides sign-up, prefills and locks the invited address from a link, and reports the acceptance outcome the register response carries. Sessions: `OPENV_SESSION_MAX_AGE` (default and ceiling 720h) and `OPENV_SESSION_IDLE` (168h), clamped with a boot log line; `GetBySessionToken` rejects a session past either bound and touches `last_seen_at` at most once a minute; the cookie MaxAge follows the absolute lifetime; the sweep deletes both kinds. `PUT /me/password` verifies the current password, applies the minimum length from one constant, stores the new hash and deletes every other session of the account (a failed purge is logged, the change stands); Personal settings carries the form. Members tab lists and revokes pending invitations and shows the one-time link. Docs: `docs/operations.md`, `docs/railway.md`, `docs/api-spec.md`, manual chapters on getting started and workspace settings.

artifacts.title: Web push: VAPID keys, per-device subscriptions and the high-signal fan-out
artifacts.body: Built (REQ-109). Migration 0026 adds `push_subscriptions` (id, user_id with `ON DELETE CASCADE`, endpoint unique, p256dh, auth, user_agent, created_at, last_used_at, failed_at) and `users.push_notifications` (default false). VAPID keys come from `OPENV_VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY`, `OPENV_VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY` and `OPENV_VAPID_SUBJECT` (mailto: or https: only); with any of them unset the feature is off and `GET /api/v1/me/push/config` answers `enabled:false`. `make vapid-keys` (`cmd/openv-vapid`) prints a fresh pair. Session-only endpoints: `POST /api/v1/me/push-subscriptions` (idempotent on the endpoint, keys refreshed, the stored row returned; the endpoint host must belong to a known push service or the `OPENV_PUSH_ENDPOINT_HOSTS` override), `DELETE` with the endpoint, `GET` listing the member's devices without their keys; `/api/v1/me/notification-prefs` carries `push_notifications` beside the email flag. Fan-out: a `PushDispatcher` beside the email dispatcher at the two dispatch points (`Notifier.deliver`, `BudgetMonitor.alertAdmins`) sends the high-signal types (`OPENV_PUSH_NOTIFICATION_TYPES` overrides the default run_failed, proposal_pending, review_requested, budget_threshold) to every subscription of an opted-in recipient through webpush-go with a 10 s HTTP timeout, from a bounded worker queue; payload `{title, body, url (same-origin path), tag type:project}`; 404/410 deletes the subscription, other failures stamp `failed_at` until the next success. The service worker gains `push` and `notificationclick` (focus and navigate an existing client, else open a window) and still caches nothing; the manifest declares two 1080×1920 screenshots and shortcuts to projects, the review queue, the board and notifications. Personal settings carries a per-device toggle that feature-detects the Push API, asks permission, subscribes with the VAPID key, reconciles with the server's device list on mount, and withdraws (server first). Docs: `docs/operations.md`, `docs/railway.md`, `docs/api-spec.md`, the manual's notifications section.

artifacts.title: Runner cards, relayed sign-in and run actions sized for a phone
artifacts.body: Built (REQ-108). The runner cards (`CloudRunnerCard`, `MyRunnerCard`, `HostedRunnerCard`) read the viewport: on a phone each fact sits under its own label (lease status, countdown with a coarse-milestone live region, pool free count) and every action is a full-width 44 px row in an `.action-sheet` column through the unchanged lease, extend and end handlers; the hosted-runner enable form is one key per row with `autoComplete="off"`, `inputMode="text"`, `autoCapitalize="none"`, `autoCorrect="off"`. The relayed sign-in (`ProviderConnectCard`) shows the authorization link as a real `target="_blank"` anchor a phone browser can follow; the paste-back field carries `enterKeyHint="send"`, submits on Enter (composition-safe), chooses `inputMode` url or text from the worker-reported `paste_kind` (regex fallback for older workers), offers a feature-detected Paste button through `navigator.clipboard.readText()`, and unlocks again when the worker refuses a code and asks for another. `RunDetailPanel` moves Cancel and Retry into a full-width 44 px pair on phones. The phone audit (`e2e/tools/phone-audit.js`) gained screens `org-runner-lease`, `runner-relay`, `run-detail-actions`, `run-detail-cancel` and `org-providers`, and now opens the settings tabs by `?tab=` (the previous tab locator matched nothing, so the runner cards had never been audited); three defects that surfaced (usage labels at 11.5 px, a member row's Leave button and the quality editor's buttons under 24 px) were fixed with a `.compact-action` class. `mobile.spec.ts` gained a step covering the runners tab control, the lease control in personal settings and the relay field's send key. Docs: `docs/plans/mobile-support.md` §8, the manual's runs and runners chapter.

artifacts.title: Uploaded profile pictures and the fixed-circle avatar
artifacts.body:
Built (REQ-133; GitHub issue #319). Migration 0033 adds `users.avatar_path` and `users.avatar_mime`, the same shape as the workspace logo: the file lives under `UPLOADS_DIR/avatars/<user id>.<ext>` and the row records where and what type. `POST /me/avatar` (multipart `file`, PNG/JPEG/GIF/WebP, bytes sniffed against the declared type, 2 MiB cap answered 413) writes the file, drops a previous file of another extension, and records path, MIME and an `avatar_url` of `/api/v1/users/{id}/avatar?v=<upload time>` through `users.Service.SetAvatar`, which touches only the avatar columns. `GET /users/{id}/avatar` serves the bytes to any signed-in session as the stored type with `nosniff`, inline, cached a day (the URL changes on every upload). `DELETE /me/avatar` removes the file and clears the three columns. `LoginWithSSO` refreshes `avatar_url` from the provider only while `avatar_path` is empty, so an uploaded picture survives sign-ins and the provider's returns after a remove. The `rasterImageExtensions` map is shared with the workspace logo.

Frontend: `Avatar` (`frontend/src/components/Avatar.tsx`) is the one picture-or-initial circle used by the workspace members tab, the project Access tab, the account menu and Personal settings; it sets `flex-shrink: 0` and a `min-width`/`min-height` floor so a long name beside it on a phone no longer squeezes it into an oval, and crops a picture with `object-fit: cover`. `resolveAvatarUrl` (`frontend/src/api/baseURL.ts`) prefixes an API-relative `avatar_url` with the API base for split deployments. Personal settings carries a Profile picture card (file input, Remove picture); the answer is written to the store's `currentUser` so every avatar on the page changes at once. Docs: `docs/api-spec.md`, `docs/data-model.md`.

artifacts.title: Release notes file, release announcement and update banner
artifacts.body:
Built (REQ-134). `RELEASE_NOTES.md` at the repository root is the customer-facing record and the version source: one `## Unreleased` section that pull requests add bullets to, then release sections newest first. A release section is headed by a semantic version and the day it shipped — `## 0.2.0 — 2026-09-14` — and groups its bullets under `### New features`, `### Maintenance updates` and `### Bug fixes`. Sections headed by a date alone (`2026-09-12`, `2026-09-12.2`) are the releases from before the numbering; they are read, never written, because `release_announcements` is keyed on the version string and renaming one would announce it again.

A root Go package (`release_notes.go`) embeds the file; `internal/domain/release` parses it. Wrapped bullets join their bullet; a level-two heading that is neither Unreleased nor a version, and a level-three heading that is not one of the three groups, are both errors; a file that fails to parse serves an empty release rather than stopping the API. `Release` carries the bullets twice — `Notes` flat for the banner and the notification, `Categories` grouped for display — and `release.Headline(version)` is the one phrasing of a release's name ("OpenV version upgraded to 0.2.0"; "OpenV update 2026-09-12" for a date-named one). `GET /api/v1/release` answers `{version, date, notes, categories, markdown, releases}` with `Cache-Control: no-store`. **The file itself is never served**: `Service.Released()` returns the parsed sections, because serving `markdown` whole once put the Unreleased section and a block of contributor instructions in front of customers.

Announcement: migration 0034 adds `release_announcements(version PK, announced_at)`. At boot, `notify.ReleaseAnnouncer` claims the current version with an insert-on-conflict-do-nothing and, when it wins, creates one `release_published` notification per account (`entity_ref.kind = release`, title from `release.Headline`, body = the first five bullets under their group headings) pushed live over SSE and handed to the email and push dispatchers, which stay in-app only unless the operator adds the type to `OPENV_EMAIL_NOTIFICATION_TYPES` / `OPENV_PUSH_NOTIFICATION_TYPES`. A restart or a second replica loses the claim and stays quiet.

Frontend: `ReleaseUpdateBanner` polls the release every 10 minutes and on visibilitychange, remembers the version it loaded with and, once a newer one answers, shows a fixed banner with a What's new link and a Reload button. `/whats-new` renders the structured `releases` — one card per release headed by `releaseHeading()`, then each group and its bullets, markdown rendered inline per bullet — never `history`. The account menu links to it and the bell routes `release` notifications there.

Pipeline: `scripts/release_notes.py` (stdlib Python, unit-tested) is the one implementation of the rules, including the version arithmetic: a release carrying anything under New features is a minor bump, one of only maintenance and fixes is a patch, `--major` is a major, and the first numbered release is 0.1.0. The `Release notes` CI job runs its self-test, checks the file's shape on every run (refusing an ungrouped bullet or an invented group), and on a pull request compares Unreleased with the base branch's copy — read leniently, so a rule added here never fails on somebody else's older file — and fails when no bullet was added, unless the PR carries the `no-release-notes` label. The Promote to release workflow cuts Unreleased into a new version section, commits that to master as the actions bot, refuses when the notes name nothing newer than what `release` carries, then pushes master and release; its `major` input is the only way the major version rises. Docs: `docs/railway.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md` (where the contributor instructions live, having been moved out of the notes file), `CLAUDE.md`, `docs/api-spec.md`, `docs/data-model.md`, `docs/operations.md`.

artifacts.title: Workspace release channel by plan
artifacts.body:
Built (REQ-136; first slice of DSC-7). Migration 0035 adds `organizations.release_channel` (TEXT, `''` = the plan's default). `internal/domain/orgs/channels.go` defines the two channels, `ChannelForPlan` (business, team and enterprise → stable; single, free, business_lite, self_host and unknown → nightly), `ChannelChoosable` (the same three company plans), and `Org.ResolveReleaseChannel`, which fills the serialised `release_channel` and `release_channel_locked` from the stored override and the plan; persistence calls it after every scan, so a stray override on a personal-tier row still resolves to nightly and reports itself locked. `Service.SetReleaseChannel` writes only that column and answers `ErrChannelLocked` for a plan that cannot choose and `ErrInvalidChannel` for an unknown name. `PUT /api/v1/orgs/{id}` accepts `release_channel` (`nightly`, `stable`, or `""` to return to the default) beside `name` and `monthly_budget_usd`; the two domain errors answer 400.

Frontend: the General tab of workspace settings gains a Release channel card that explains the workspace's channel, names the running release from `GET /api/v1/release`, and, for an admin of a company plan, offers a Stable / Nightly select that updates the workspace in the store. Personal-tier workspaces see the channel and the sentence that their plan always runs nightly.

Not in this slice: nothing is gated by channel yet and the release announcement still reaches every account; those are steps 2 and 3 of the plan in DSC-7. Docs: `docs/release-policy.md` (the approved policy and implementation status), `docs/api-spec.md`, `docs/data-model.md`, `CLAUDE.md`.

artifacts.title: Feature gates by channel and per-channel release notifications
artifacts.body:
Built (REQ-137, REQ-140; steps 2 and 3 of DSC-7). `internal/domain/release/features.go` is the registry: a `Feature{Key, ShippedIn, Summary}` declares the release version it first shipped in. `Enabled(feature, channel, stableRelease)` is the rule: the nightly channel sees everything; the stable channel sees a feature once the stable release the workspace has turned on is that version or a later one (`release.AtOrBefore`, which orders semantic versions and the dated releases from before them), and nothing while the workspace has no stable release. `FeaturesFor(service, channel, stableVersion)` resolves the whole registry and closes every gate for a version the notes do not mark as stable. `GET /api/v1/orgs/{id}/features` answers the caller's gates (`channel`, `stable_release`, `preview`, `features`, and the next scheduled stable with its time); the server-side `featureEnabled(r, orgID, key)` gates handlers; the frontend loads the gates into the store per active workspace and `useFeature(key)` answers false until they are loaded so a gated screen never flashes on. Requests without a session (workers, agent runs) see everything.

The notes groups decide what is gated: a bullet under *New features* is a change stable-channel workspaces wait for; *Maintenance updates* and *Bug fixes* reach every channel with the release that carries them and are never gated. There is no per-bullet marker.

Notifications follow the channel: the boot-time announcer (`notify.ReleaseAnnouncer`) tells only accounts with a nightly-channel workspace (`orgs.ListMemberUserIDsByChannel`, effective channel computed in SQL from the plan and the override), with the grouped copy of REQ-134; stable-channel members are told by the stable scheduler when their release turns on (DES-45). What's new opens with the active workspace's own channel line (the stable release it runs and the one scheduled next, or the release it runs), then the grouped history with stable releases badged.

artifacts.title: Stable releases: monthly designation, upgrade window, preview and scheduler
artifacts.body:
Built (REQ-135, REQ-138, REQ-140; steps 3 and 4 of DSC-7). A stable release is one of the numbered releases in `RELEASE_NOTES.md`, designated by a marker line straight under its heading: `Stable channel release since <date>.` (`release.StableMarker`). The Go parser records it as `Release.StableSince`, keeps it out of the notes and body, and `Notes.CurrentStable()` / `Notes.Stable(version)` build a `Stable{Version, Since, Previous, Notes, Categories}` whose notes are every release after the previous stable up to this one, merged group by group in reading order (releases from before version numbers are never merged in). `scripts/release_notes.py cut-stable` designates the newest release whose heading date is at least seven days before the cut date and that is newer than the current stable (`--fix`: the newest release, no soak; `--if-scheduled`: a no-op on weekends or when the month already has a designation), refuses when nothing newer has soaked, and inserts only the marker line. The *Cut stable release* workflow (`cut-stable.yml`) runs at 06:00 UTC on the 1st to 3rd, cuts anything pending as a release first ("Release <v>"), designates ("Stable release <v>"), and pushes master and release so the API boots on the new notes.

Migration 0036 adds `organizations.stable_release`, `upgrade_day`, `upgrade_hour`, `upgrade_timezone` and `org_members.preview_next_stable`; migration 0037 adds `release_schedule(org_id, version, announced_at, reminded_at, turned_on_at)`, each column set only while NULL so every step is claimed once. `orgs.UpgradeTimeFor(since, day, hour, tz)` is the rule: no window means at the designation; otherwise the first day-of-month/hour in the zone after it, clamped to 14 days after. `notify.StableScheduler` runs at boot and hourly over `ListOrgsByChannel(stable)`: for a workspace whose `stable_release` is older than the newest stable (`release.Newer`) it tells the admins at the designation (`release_scheduled`, with the turn-on time and a count of new features and other changes), reminds them 24 hours before (windowed workspaces only), and at the turn-on sets `stable_release` and tells every member with the merged notes in the grouped announcement copy (`release_published`). `PUT /orgs/{id}` accepts `upgrade_window` (`{day 1-28, hour, timezone}` or null; `ErrInvalidWindow` / `ErrChannelLocked` answer 400), `PUT /orgs/{id}/members/me/preview` switches the caller's own gates to the newest stable, and the features endpoint reports `next_stable_release` and `next_stable_at`. `GET /api/v1/release` carries `stable` (the merged stable) and marks stable releases in `releases` with `stable_since`. Workspace settings carry the window form (day, hour, IANA zone defaulting to the browser's) and the preview checkbox, and show the running and next stable.

artifacts.title: Release feed, dedicated support window, nightly automation and the route inventory
artifacts.body:
Built (REQ-139, REQ-141, REQ-143; steps 5 to 7 of DSC-7). `GET /api/v1/public/release` is the open feed `{version, stable, stable_since}` (the release the shared service runs, its newest stable, and the day that stable was designated), cacheable five minutes. A server started with `OPENV_DEPLOYMENT=dedicated` runs `notify.SupportWindowWatcher`: daily it reads `OPENV_RELEASE_FEED_URL` (default the shared service's feed) and, when the feed's stable is newer than its own, computes the window close as the feed stable's designation date plus 90 days and warns every workspace's admins (`release_support_window`) once at 30 days, once at 7 and once after the close, each claimed in `release_announcements` under a `support-window:<stable>:<n>` key. `GET /api/v1/release` reports `deployment`. `docs/railway.md` describes a dedicated instance as this deployment checked out at the commit that designated a stable release.

Which build is running: `GET /api/v1/public/build` answers `{commit}` and the frontend serves `/build.json` with the same field, both from `RAILWAY_GIT_COMMIT_SHA` at deploy time (`OPENV_BUILD_SHA` overrides it; with neither set the value is empty, leaving local runs and the compose stack unchanged). The API's `GET /health` carries `commit` too, for Railway's healthcheck and for a caller that can reach the API directly.

The gate reads the `/api/` route rather than `/health` because the staging URL is the **frontend's** origin: `frontend/nginx.conf` answers `/health` itself with plain `healthy` and proxies only `/api/`, so the API's `/health` is unreachable from there. The build route is `no-store` — a deploy that has just landed is exactly what the caller is waiting to notice — while the release feed beside it keeps its five-minute cache and its dedicated-instance consumers. It sits under `/api/v1/public/`, which `isOpenPath` already exempts from auth, so CI reads it with no credentials. Two endpoints, API and frontend, because they are separate Railway builds that finish at different times: a new API behind the previous frontend fails the journey on a UI string the commit changed.

Staging: a second Railway environment on `master` while production stays on `release`, with its own Postgres and volume, its own URL variables, `OPENV_NOINDEX=1` on the frontend, and no SMTP, VAPID or Google credentials, so no mail, push or SSO callback can leave a test run. `OPENV_REGISTRATION=closed` after a two-step bootstrap (register the maintainer and the smoke account while sign-up is open, then close it), which is what admits only maintainers and previewing customers. `docs/railway.md` "Staging" carries the build-out, including the check that forked variables are still `${{…}}` references — a fork copies them verbatim, and a rendered `DATABASE_URL` literal would make staging boot and migrate against the production database.
