  `/api` on the same origin. Then the cookie is first-party,
  `CROSS_SITE_COOKIES` comes off, `SameSite=Lax` applies, CORS is unused, and
  the CSP `connect-src` collapses to `'self'`. Self-hosted compose can do the
  same or keep two ports.
- **B. A custom domain pair** (`app.example` and `api.example`) under one
  registrable domain, keeping CORS. Needs a domain and DNS; still cross-origin
  for CORS purposes but same-site for cookies.

Belt and braces in the same PR: set the `Partitioned` attribute (CHIPS) on
the session and OIDC cookies when `CROSS_SITE_COOKIES` is on, so any
remaining cross-site deployment works on Safari 18.4 and later. Add a WebKit
project and an iPhone project to Playwright so the sign-in journey is run on
the engine that failed.

Effort: one to two days. Risk: SSE through nginx (buffering), upload size
cap, and `/api/v1/public/connector/download` (27 MB) through the proxy;
keep that one on the API origin or raise the cap for it.

### Phase 1 — Layout foundation

Make the shell responsive without redesigning any view.

- A `useViewport` hook and two breakpoints: phone (≤ 640 px) and narrow
  tablet (≤ 900 px), exposed as a context so views can branch.
- `ProjectLayout`: below the phone breakpoint the side navigation becomes an
  off-canvas drawer behind a 44 px menu button; the auto-hide mode is treated
  as hidden on touch; edge strips grow to 44 px.
- The requirements workspace: below the tablet breakpoint the three columns
  become one stacked view with a segmented control (Tree, Document, Notes),
  each scrolling within its own bounds, so REQ-53's fit-the-window contract
  holds on every width instead of clipping.
- The guided wizard: rail collapses to a top progress bar; the assistant
  panel becomes a bottom sheet.
- Global fixes: `100dvh` and safe-area insets; 16 px inputs; every table in
  an `overflow-x: auto` wrapper; login and the unclamped modals capped at
  the viewport; `viewport-fit=cover` and the Apple web-app meta tags;
  `autoComplete` on the login form; `enterKeyHint` on chat composers.

Effort: three to five days.

### Phase 2 — The mobile jobs

Make the review-and-act flows first class on a phone, in this order:

1. **Review queue and proposals**: card list with approve, reject and open
   actions; the proposal diff readable at 360 px.
2. **Notifications**: the bell becomes a full-screen list; deep links land
   on mobile views.
3. **Reading requirements**: the stacked workspace from Phase 1 plus a
   reference search that jumps to a ref; comments and the V&V Assistant on
   the same chat skeleton the interview page uses.
4. **Board**: one column at a time with a pager; a card's action sheet
   offers *Move to…* and *Assign to agent*, so launching an agent no longer
   depends on drag.
5. **Runner card**: start, extend and end a cloud runner; the relayed
   sign-in screen sized for a phone (this is where a paste from a password
   manager has to work).
6. **Runs**: list, detail, retry and cancel.

Effort: one to two weeks.

### Phase 3 — Touch parity for editing

- A kebab button on every artifact row opens the same menu as right-click.
- *Move to…* dialog (choose parent and position) as the touch alternative to
  drag, using the existing `planMove` logic.
- Convert drags to pointer events with `touch-action: none` on the handle,
  so tree and board drag also work with a finger where the screen allows it.
- Figure actions always visible on touch devices; the figure reference
  autocomplete gets a tap-to-insert menu.

Effort: about a week.

### Phase 4 — Installability and polish

- Manifest screenshots and shortcuts (Review queue, Board, Notifications).
- Web Push for the high-signal notification types: a VAPID key pair, a
  push-subscription table, a subscribe endpoint, and the service worker's
  `push` handler; opt-in per device.
- `prefers-reduced-motion`; raise the muted-text contrast token to 4.5:1;
  a server-side thumbnail size for figures and a right-sized logo.

Effort: about a week, of which push is most of it.

## 5. Testing

- Playwright projects: Desktop Chrome (existing), WebKit, iPhone 13,
  Pixel 5, iPad portrait. The smoke journey runs on all of them; a mobile
  journey covers sign-in, review queue approve, board move via action sheet,
  and starting a cloud runner up to the relay screen.
- A viewport contract test: at 360 px wide no view scrolls horizontally and
  every primary action is at least 44 px.
- Lighthouse mobile in CI as an informational score, not a gate.

## 6. Requirements recorded

NEED-13 *Act on my product from my phone* and, deriving from it, REQ-101
same-site session, REQ-102 responsive shell, REQ-103 stacked requirements
workspace, REQ-104 touch alternatives for every drag, hover and right-click
action, REQ-105 tap targets and input sizing, REQ-106 mobile review and
approval, REQ-107 board actions without drag, REQ-108 runner control from a
phone, REQ-109 installable app metadata and push, REQ-110 mobile test
coverage; DES-23 same-origin API proxy; TC-50 mobile journey suite.

## 7. Decisions for the maintainer

1. Phase 0 option A (nginx proxy, recommended) or B (custom domain pair).
2. Whether Web Push is worth its backend surface now or waits.
3. Whether a store presence will ever matter (it changes nothing in Phases
   0 to 3; it decides whether Phase 4 grows a Capacitor wrapper).

## 8. Implementation status (2026-09-07)

Decisions taken: Phase 0 option A (nginx proxy); Web Push deferred; no
store presence planned.

Shipped, in one PR on top of this plan:

- **Phase 0** — `frontend/nginx.conf` proxies `/api/` to `API_UPSTREAM`
  (re-resolved through the container's DNS by
  `frontend/docker-entrypoint.d/40-openv-api-proxy.sh`); the client defaults
  to a relative `/api` in production builds; the CSP collapses to `'self'`;
  `Partitioned` on cross-site cookies; a WebKit Playwright project. The
  connector download goes through the proxy unbuffered, so no special case
  was needed. Production needs the variable changes in `docs/railway.md`
  (`API_UPSTREAM` on the frontend; `CROSS_SITE_COOKIES` off and `PUBLIC_URL`
  on the frontend origin for the API) at the next promotion.
- **Phase 1** — `hooks/useViewport`; drawer navigation with a top bar below
  900 px; the stacked Tree / Document / Notes requirements module; the
  wizard's progress strip and assistant bottom sheet; 16 px fields on touch,
  `100dvh`, table wrappers, safe-area helpers, reduced motion, clamped login
  and modals, viewport and installed-app meta tags.
- **Phase 2** — notifications panel full-width on phones; suspect links as
  cards with 44 px controls; the board shows one column at a time with a
  pager and a card actions sheet offering *Open card* and *Move to <column>*
  (the same move as a drop, so it launches an agent from To Do). Runs,
  proposals and the requirements page reuse the stacked layout and table
  wrappers rather than new mobile views.
- **Phase 3** — every artifact row has a visible ⋯ actions button opening
  the right-click menu; the menu gains *Move to…* (target artifact and
  before / after / inside, validated by `planMove`); on coarse pointers a
  grip handle drags rows through pointer events with `touch-action: none`
  on the handle only, so the list still scrolls.
- **Phase 4 (part)** — manifest shortcuts and categories; muted text raised
  to 4.6:1; reduced-motion media query.
- **Testing** — `e2e/tests/mobile.spec.ts` runs in iPhone 13 (WebKit) and
  Pixel 5 (Chromium) projects: drawer navigation, the stacked module, and
  the no-horizontal-scroll contract on every page it visits.

Deferred, each a follow-up of its own:

- Web Push (VAPID keys, a subscription table, a subscribe endpoint, the
  worker's `push` handler) — REQ-109 remains partially met (installable,
  no push).
- The runner card and the relayed sign-in screen sized for a phone
  (REQ-108); they work through the responsive shell but were not reworked.
- Figure actions on touch and the tap-to-insert reference menu; server-side
  figure thumbnails; manifest screenshots; an iPad project and Lighthouse in
  CI.

artifacts.title: Mobile readiness assessment 2026-09-07
artifacts.body:
Scope: `frontend/` at `81030f9` (master after PR #298). 35,511 lines of
TS/TSX across 7 CSS files; styling is overwhelmingly inline `style={{}}`
objects, so almost nothing is reachable by a media query. Companion to
`docs/plans/mobile-support.md`.

**Headline: the app is a desktop-only application.** There is no responsive
layer, no touch layer, and on the production Railway topology no working
sign-in on iOS Safari. It is installable as a PWA, but the installed app is
the same desktop layout.

## 1. Responsive design

Exactly ten `@media` occurrences, six of them responsive, all in leaf
components: `ImageLightbox.css:88`, `ImageGallery.css:145`,
`ProjectList.css:331`, `ImageUploadInput.css:57` (all `max-width: 768px`)
and `HelpSidebar.css:179,189` (1024 and 768 px). No layout container has
one. No component reads the screen width: a grep for `innerWidth`,
`matchMedia`, `ResizeObserver`, `visualViewport` finds only the theme's
`prefers-color-scheme` check.

Fixed-pixel layouts that decide the minimum usable width:

| View | Fixed widths | Minimum before content is legible |
|---|---|---|
| `ProjectLayout.tsx:171-212` | shell `100vh`/`overflow:hidden`; nav `width/minWidth 200`; edge strip 10 px | 200 px before any view |
| `ModuleView.tsx:1084-1750` | tree column 400 px default (`min 200`, `max 800`), notes 320 px (`min 250`), two 10 px resize handles, 40 px padding, `overflow: hidden` | about 460 px with the document pane at zero |
| `GuidedWizard.tsx:1654-1677` + `StepShell.tsx:43` + `GuidedChatPanel.tsx:510` | rail 220 px, chat panel 340 px, no `flexWrap` | 852 px with the nav |
| `KanbanBoard.tsx:325-345` | columns `flex: 0 0 260px`, row scrolls horizontally | one column visible on a phone |
| `TraceabilityMatrix.tsx:226-303` | pinned 240 px column, further `minWidth` 200 to 280 | about 1160 px |
| `CrewBuilder.tsx:669`, `AgentsPage.tsx:138`, `AgentRunsPage.tsx:330`, `ImpactView.tsx:112`, `ManualView.tsx:164-169` | side panels of 320, 320, 460, 320 and 260 px | two-column with no fallback |
| `Login.tsx:72`, `CreateOrgModal.tsx:65`, `WorkItemDrawer.tsx:150` | 380, 400 and 420 px with no `maxWidth` | overflow on an iPhone SE |

The shared `Modal`, `ConfirmDialog` and `PromptDialog` are correctly clamped
to the viewport. Twelve of fifteen tables have fixed-width headers and no
horizontal scroll wrapper. `100vh` is used in about ten places where
`100dvh` is needed.

The `overflow: hidden` shell is REQ-53's fit-the-window contract working as
designed; on a narrow screen it converts every overflow into clipped,
unreachable content rather than a scroll.

## 2. Touch and pointer

- Every drag is HTML5 `draggable` plus `dataTransfer`
  (`ArtifactList.tsx:213-272`, `KanbanBoard.tsx:331-377`); a grep for
  touch or pointer handlers in `src/` finds none. Touch browsers do not
  synthesise these events. Reparenting an artifact is drag-only
  (`utils/artifactDrag.ts:10-13`) and launching an agent from the board is
  drag-only (`KanbanBoard.tsx:320`).
- The Cytoscape crew canvas (`CrewCanvas.tsx:165-340`) is the one exception
  and already handles tap and drag by touch, with 30 px nodes.
- The artifact context menu is right-click only (`ArtifactList.tsx:207-212`)
  and carries seven actions with no other entry point; iOS shows its native
  callout on long-press instead of firing `contextmenu`.
- Panel auto-hide opens on hover (`panelMode.ts:47`), is persisted per
  person, and is recovered through a 10 px strip; on touch it behaves as
  hidden. Figure actions sit in a hover overlay (`ImageGallery.css:43-45`).
  Column resizing binds mouse events only (`ModuleView.tsx:151-197`).
- 151 `title` tooltips never render on touch; several carry the only
  explanation of a control.
- Tap targets: edge strips and resize handles 10 px; tree chevron 14 px;
  download-wizard checkboxes 16 px; nav section headers about 26 px tall;
  most chips `padding: 1px 6px`. Only the help button (60 px) and the
  interview composer (44 px) meet the 44 px guideline. 117 `fontSize`
  values of 11 px or less.

## 3. Viewport and PWA

`index.html` has a correct viewport meta without `user-scalable=no`, a
theme colour, one apple-touch-icon and the manifest link; it lacks
`viewport-fit=cover` and the Apple web-app meta tags. `manifest.json` is
complete: `display: standalone`, `id`, `start_url`, `scope`, maskable and
plain icons at 192 and 512 px; no screenshots or shortcuts, and
`orientation: any` lets an installed phone app launch into a portrait layout
it cannot render. `sw.js` deliberately caches nothing (documented
rationale: live collaborative app), so there is no offline mode, no push,
and no stale-shell risk; registration is inline in `index.tsx:30-37`.

## 4. Navigation

`ProjectLayout` is a permanent 200 px left rail with no drawer, hamburger
or tab bar. `panelMode` is a preference, not a response to width; the
default is pinned. Nothing adapts to the screen.

## 5. Mobile-specific views

`InterviewChat.tsx` is the only phone-first screen: a fluid column capped at
640 px, the standard header, scrolling list and fixed composer, 80 percent
bubbles with word wrapping, a 44 px composer, no cookie (`withCredentials:
false`), so it works on iOS. Its faults are `100vh`, a 14 px textarea
(focus zoom) and a Ctrl-Enter-only shortcut beside the send button.

## 6. Inputs

`index.css:116-125` sets 14 px on every input, textarea and select, so iOS
zooms on focus and stays zoomed; several components go to 12 or 13 px. The
body editor's `#` reference autocomplete is driven by arrow, Enter and Tab
keys (`ArtifactEditor.tsx:196-211`), none of which a soft keyboard offers,
though entries can be tapped. No `capture` attribute on file inputs, which
is correct (the OS offers camera and library). No date inputs exist. No
`inputMode`, `autoCapitalize` or `enterKeyHint`; `autoComplete` only appears
as `off`, so the login form gets no password-manager autofill.

## 7. Authentication on mobile

`api/client.ts:34-41` is cookie-only (`withCredentials: true`) with no
bearer fallback. Production sets `CROSS_SITE_COOKIES=true`, so
`handlers.go:187-192` issues the session as `SameSite=None; Secure`. The two
`up.railway.app` hosts are different registrable sites (the suffix is on the
Public Suffix List), so the cookie is third-party. Safari blocks third-party
cookies unconditionally and every iOS browser is WebKit: sign-in appears to
succeed, the next request answers 401, and the response interceptor
(`client.ts:70-79`) sends the user back to the login page. The cookie is not
`Partitioned` (Go's `http.Cookie` field is unused), Safari also caps
`SameSite=None` lifetimes, and the three `EventSource` streams inherit the
same problem. The public interview route is the one flow that works.
Self-hosted deployments on one domain get `SameSite=Lax` and are unaffected.

## 8. Performance

No client-side PDF or DOCX libraries (exports are server-side). Routes are
code-split well (`App.tsx:28-59`): the 1.1 MB ag-grid chunk and the 434 KB
Cytoscape chunk stay off the first load. The main bundle is 616 KB
uncompressed and first render waits on three sequential API calls. The
navbar logo is a 180 KB PNG drawn at 56 px; gallery thumbnails load
full-resolution attachments; no `loading="lazy"` or `srcSet` anywhere; gzip
on, brotli off; source maps are shipped.

## 9. Accessibility that affects mobile

Pinch-zoom is preserved; the token system supports dark mode and
`prefers-color-scheme`; body text contrast is strong. The muted text token
(`#7f8c8d` on white) is about 3.6:1, below AA, and it is used for much of
the small secondary text; `--neutral` on white is about 2.6:1. No
`prefers-reduced-motion` handling; the board's live-run indicator pulses
indefinitely.

## 10. Tests

`e2e/playwright.config.ts` has one project, Desktop Chrome. No WebKit, no
device profile, no viewport override. Nothing in CI exercises the engine
where the cookie blocker lives.

## Ranked obstacles

Phone: (1) sign-in impossible on iOS; (2) no responsive layer; (3) the
requirements workspace clips at any width under about 460 px; (4) all drag
dead on touch with no alternative for reparenting or handing a card to an
agent; (5) right-click-only artifact menu; (6) focus zoom on every field;
(7) the login card overflows small phones; (8) 10 to 24 px tap targets on
the controls that recover panels and expand branches; (9) auto-hide panel
mode is a trap on touch; (10) the guided wizard needs 852 px.

Tablet: (1) the iOS cookie blocker; (2) drag still dead, on a layout that
otherwise fits; (3) right-click and hover-only actions; (4) portrait breaks
the three-column views and the manifest allows portrait; (5) column
resizing and panel recovery are mouse-only.

artifacts.title: Desktop viewports from 1024 to 3840 pixels
artifacts.body: At every viewport width from 1024 pixels to 3840 pixels the system shall show each screen without horizontal scrolling of the page. At every such width the system shall clip no control. At every such width the system shall render each clickable control at least 24 pixels high. At every such width the system shall render no visible text smaller than 12 pixels. At a viewport width of 1024 pixels the requirements workspace shall keep the document pane at least 400 pixels wide while the tree and notes columns are visible. On a viewport wider than 1600 pixels the system shall limit a reading surface (an artifact document, an editor, a settings card) to a measure of 1100 pixels or less. On a viewport wider than 1600 pixels the system shall limit a single-line field inside a reading surface to a width of 720 pixels or less. At a device pixel ratio of 2 the system shall draw each raster image at or below its native pixel width.

artifacts.title: Release structure and channel policy 2026-09-12
artifacts.body:
# Release structure and channel policy

Status: **approved by the maintainer 2026-09-12**, with the recommended
route (option B for the shared service, option C for enterprise pinning,
no annual release, staging after the alpha). Requirements recorded under
**Release channels** (NEED-15, REQ-135 … REQ-143). The repository copy of
the policy and its implementation status is `docs/release-policy.md`.
Builds on what shipped in REQ-134: releases cut from `RELEASE_NOTES.md`,
announced to every account, with open tabs offering a reload.

Amended 2026-09-13: releases are numbered by semantic version derived from
the notes (REQ-143, shipped as 0.1.0), so the stable channel is expressed
on that scheme rather than on calendar versions. See section 4.

## 1. The question

Now that every promotion is a named release that members are told about,
should business and enterprise workspaces be able to pin a release and
choose their upgrade schedule, while personal and lite workspaces ride the
latest release? And what release structure should OpenV follow: nightly,
monthly minor, annual major?

## 2. What constrains the answer

- **One shared multi-tenant service.** Every workspace on the Railway
  deployment runs against one Postgres database with forward-only
  migrations. Running two code versions against that database at once
  means every migration must stay compatible with the older version for as
  long as it is still serving anyone (expand, migrate, then contract), and
  a member with a personal workspace and a business workspace would be
  using two different builds through one sign-in. Per-workspace pinning of
  *code* on the shared service is therefore the expensive option.
- **Self-hosting already exists.** The compose stack and the Railway recipe
  are the same product an enterprise can run on its own; an enterprise
  that needs a release held still already has a way to get exactly that.
- **The team is small and releases are cheap.** Promotion is one workflow
  run; release notes are cut automatically; the risk of a release is
  bounded by CI, the E2E smoke and, after alpha, a staging soak.

## 3. Options considered

| Option | What it means | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| A. Per-workspace code pinning on the shared service | Route each workspace to a deployment of its pinned version; shared database | Rejected: multi-version schema compatibility on every migration, two builds behind one sign-in, and a fleet of deployments to keep patched. |
| B. Channels on one deployment, with feature gating | Everyone runs the latest build; new features are switched on per workspace by channel (nightly at the release, stable at the monthly designation); maintenance and fixes reach everyone at once | **Approved.** This is how large multi-tenant products deliver "stable": the code is one, the experience is staged. Upgrade windows become a per-workspace timer, not a deployment. |
| C. Dedicated instance pinned to a release | Enterprise runs its own instance (self-hosted or single-tenant hosted) on a stable release and upgrades on its own date | **Approved for enterprise only.** True pinning, a staging copy to try the next release, and a support window that bounds how far behind it may fall. |
| D. Annual major releases (LTS) | One release a year with backports | Deferred. It commits a small team to a year of backports before any customer has asked; breaking changes are handled by deprecation windows across stable releases, and a major version is cut only when one is deliberately declared. Revisit when a paying enterprise asks for it. |

## 4. Structure

| Channel | Cadence | Version | Who |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Nightly** (latest) | Every promotion of a green master with new notes; automated nightly at 03:00 UTC once staging exists, plus manual runs | Semantic, derived from the notes: a new feature is a minor bump (0.2.0), maintenance and fixes a patch (0.2.1), a major is asked for (REQ-143) | Personal and Lite, always. Business may opt in. |
| **Stable** (monthly) | On the first working day of the month, the newest release that has served the nightly channel for at least 7 days and is newer than the current stable is designated the stable release by a marker line under its heading in the notes; not a separate build. Its notes for stable-channel members are every release since the previous stable, merged group by group | The release's own version | Business by default; Enterprise on the shared service. |
| **Dedicated** | Enterprise instance on a stable release; upgraded on the customer's date within 90 days of the next stable, previewed on the customer's staging copy first | The stable version it runs | Enterprise that needs pinning. |

Semantic versioning throughout, with the version derived from the notes.
The API, the MCP tools and the exports stay backward compatible across
stable releases, and a removal is announced in two consecutive stable
releases before it happens.

Security fixes go to every channel at the next nightly and, by a manual
run of the stable workflow with `fix: true`, become the stable release the
same day; they are never held by a schedule.

## 5. What business and enterprise get to choose

- **Upgrade window** (shared service): the day of the month and hour, in
  the workspace's time zone, at which the monthly release turns on for the
  workspace, up to 14 days after the designation. Admins are notified at
  the designation with the notes, and again 24 hours before the turn-on.
  Until then the workspace keeps the previous month's behaviour.
- **Preview**: a workspace admin can turn the next stable on early for
  themselves alone to try it, without moving the workspace.
- **Dedicated**: choose the upgrade date within the 90-day window, with the
  target release running on the customer's staging copy beforehand; the
  platform warns when an instance is about to leave the window.

Personal and Lite are on nightly and cannot change it. That is the trade
they make for the lower tier: newest features first, and they carry the
risk of a nightly. The staging soak and the reload banner keep that risk
small and visible.

## 6. Staging (after alpha)

A staging environment deployed from every merge to master, on its own
database seeded with anonymised data. The nightly promotion is gated on
that commit's E2E smoke passing on staging and its migrations having
applied cleanly there. Staging is also where an enterprise's next stable
is previewed and where the maintainer checks a release by hand before a
monthly designation.

## 7. Implementation plan

1. **Workspace release channel** (REQ-136) — shipped 2026-09-12 (DES-43,
   TC-71): channel derived from plan, admin-selectable on company plans,
   shown in workspace settings with the running release.
2. **Feature gating by channel** (REQ-137) — built (DES-44, TC-72): a
   feature registry keyed on the release a feature shipped in, resolved
   against the workspace's turned-on stable; New features is the gated
   group, maintenance and fixes are not; the nightly announcement goes only
   to members of nightly-channel workspaces (REQ-140 part one).
3. **Stable releases in the pipeline** (REQ-135, REQ-140) — built (DES-45,
   TC-73): the monthly *Cut stable release* workflow designates a soaked
   release by the marker line; stable-channel members are notified at their
   upgrade time with the notes since the previous stable; What's new opens
   with the workspace's own channel and marks stable releases.
4. **Upgrade window and personal preview** (REQ-138) — built (DES-45,
   TC-73): per-workspace turn-on time, the 24-hour reminder, and the
   admin's own early switch.
5. **Staging and nightly automation** (REQ-141, REQ-135) — workflow in
   place (DES-46), a no-op until the staging environment exists after the
   alpha: a Railway staging environment fed from master, the smoke gate,
   and the 03:00 UTC promotion.
6. **Dedicated instances** (REQ-139) — built (DES-46, TC-74): the
   support-window warnings from the public release feed; the staging copy
   once the single-tenant offer exists.
7. **Compatibility rule** (REQ-143) — enforced (DES-46): the route
   inventory test pins the HTTP surface.

artifacts.title: Flow-down, ownership and supplier subsets 2026-09-13
artifacts.body:
# Flow-down, ownership and supplier subsets

Requested by the maintainer 2026-09-13: on a large programme, or when a
subset of the work is outsourced, requirements flow down between projects
(the A350 has requirements; the landing gear has its own; each component
has its own), validation flows down and verification flows up along links,
and owners within a project let a subset be exported quickly. Owners must
include reference parties a project can add, with the workspace's own
company on the list by default. Behaviour cross-referenced with DOORS and
its competitors. Recorded as NEED-16 and REQ-144 to REQ-148; repository
guide `docs/flow-down.md`.

## 1. What the competitors do

| | IBM DOORS / DOORS Next | Jama Connect | Polarion | Codebeamer |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hierarchy | Folders and modules; project areas in DOORS Next | Projects, components, sets | Project groups | Project trees |
| Cross-project links | Link modules; cross-project links with global configurations | Relationships across projects; reuse and sync | Cross-project work-item links | Cross-project references |
| Verification roll-up | Views and reports per module; no automatic roll-up across projects | Coverage per item; cross-project coverage through views | Traceability reports | Coverage reports |
| Owner | User attributes; a partition names the partner | Assignee, organisation fields | Assignee | Assigned to |
| Supplier subset | **Partitions**: export a subset of modules to a partner, who edits and returns it, then synchronise | Baselines and exports per view | Exports per query | Exports per filter |

DOORS partitions are the closest fit to the outsourcing case, and they are
round-trip. Nobody rolls verification up across a project tree
automatically; each tool leaves that to reports.

## 2. Decisions

- **One tree of projects, not modules within a project.** OpenV's unit of
  access is the project (REQ-16), so a supplier is simply a member of the
  child project. A project names its parent; a parent must be in the same
  workspace and may not be a descendant.
- **Flow-down is a link type, `refines`, allowed to cross projects.** It
  is created from the child with editor rights there and viewer rights on
  the parent, since a supplier can only read what it refines. Every other
  cross-project link type keeps editor rights on both ends.
- **A link belongs to both projects it touches.** Links were listed by the
  source artifact's project alone, which hid a flow-down link from the
  parent. Listing by either end fixes the parent's export, baseline,
  coverage, matrix and map at once; the far end is described by a
  `linked_artifacts` list (project name, reference, title) so no rights
  on the other project are needed to name it.
- **Verification rolls up automatically.** A parent requirement's
  coverage carries its refinements' rollups, computed in their own
  projects recursively, and the worst of them. A requirement with no
  evidence of its own is verified through its refinements; one with
  evidence keeps the worse; one without a method stays method-missing.
  This is the one place OpenV goes further than the tools compared.
- **Owner is a standard attribute, matched by name.** A person, a team
  or a supplier, so a vendor with no account here can own requirements.
  Each project keeps reference parties; the workspace's own company is
  always first (never stored, always implied). Members are offered too.
- **Subsets are an owners filter on every download**, the outbound half
  of a DOORS partition. Bringing a supplier's edits back is a re-import
  matched on stable references: not built, the next step.
- **Both features are gated** (REQ-137): keys `flow-down` and
  `artifact-owners` ship in 0.3.0, so stable-channel workspaces receive
  them at their next stable release.

## 3. Status

Built 2026-09-13: DES-47 (hierarchy, refines, both-end links, flow-up),
DES-48 (owners, parties, owner-filtered downloads); verified by TC-75 and
TC-76.

artifacts.title: Billing and tiers plan 2026-09-21
artifacts.body:
# Stripe billing in-app, and making the tiers real

Status: approved 2026-09-21, nothing implemented yet. The full text lives in
the repository at `docs/plans/billing-stripe.md` (commit e58f8c1); this
artifact carries the decisions and the phase structure so the requirements
that follow have something to derive from. It supersedes the Odoo proposal
in `docs/billing-odoo.md`.

## 1. The two problems

**There is no way to buy anything.** The previous design put Odoo in the
middle. That is superseded: Stripe direct, in the app. Stripe Tax and Stripe
Invoicing cover the tax and invoicing that were Odoo's justification;
enterprise sales and CRM go by email for now.

**The tiers are not real.** Outside `internal/domain/orgs/limits.go` and
`channels.go`, the only plan check in the Go codebase is the open-source
baseline check. Every count limit ships at 0 = unlimited on every plan. Of
everything the pricing page sells as paid, exactly two things are enforced —
cloud-runner resource numbers and the release channel. Always-on hosted
runners, teams, per-project access grants, shared company workspaces,
workspace budgets and usage rollups are all free today.

**Who pays.** A quality lead or engineering manager at a small regulated
firm who will not run Postgres, backups, TLS and upgrades and would not be
allowed to. Self-hosting being free under ELv2 does not make gates pointless
for that buyer; the people who self-host were never going to pay and are
worth more as references. The paid layer is the company layer — seats,
shared workspaces, teams, per-project grants, budget rollups, unattended
hosted compute. The product itself (traceability, baselines, history, V&V,
export, agent runs on your own AI) stays free.

## 2. Decisions taken

| | |
|---|---|
| Provider | Stripe direct. No Odoo, no CRM |
| Purchase surface | Stripe Checkout, redirect, returning to a Billing tab in workspace settings |
| Tax | Stripe Tax; OpenV stays merchant of record (we register and file) |
| Self-serve tiers | `business_lite` (hard-coded quantity 1, never seat-synced) and `business` (per-seat) |
| Enterprise | Email → platform-admin plan endpoint (REQ-154) → invoice by hand. Never a Stripe subscription |
| Seats | Member count leads; quantity pushed after the fact; Stripe prorates. Business only |
| Trial | 14 days, card up front, one trial per buyer, promotion codes on |
| Currencies | GBP, USD, EUR via `currency_options`; a customer's currency is fixed by its first purchase |
| Sync | Poll-only at launch: one paginated subscription list per 5-minute tick plus a synchronous post-checkout refresh. No webhook receiver until a staleness metric says the poll cannot keep up |
| Moves to paid | Unattended hosted compute → Lite; shared workspaces + seats, teams and per-project grants, workspace budget + usage rollups → Business |
| Hosted compute | Metered: 300 hosted-runner minutes/month on free, unlimited on paid. Runs via the Agent Connector on the user's own machine are never metered |
| Free taste | One shared workspace created by you, two members (creator + one) |
| Over plan | Read-only: existing work readable and exportable, not editable, until the workspace upgrades or trims. Nothing is ever deleted |
| Grandfathering | Workspaces created before a date announced with the first live price keep alpha terms forever, enforced by per-workspace limit overrides written by a migration |
| Phases | 1) plumbing + client + read-only sync; 2) checkout; 3) seat sync; 4) gates + numbers + grandfather |

## 3. Non-goals

No `402` — resource refusals keep 403 `limit_reached`. No new Railway
service. No plan-gated export or import in any state, including read-only
(REQ-113). No cap on projects beyond an abuse ceiling. No gate on baselines,
version history, traceability, flow-down, V&V, sign-in methods, MCP/connector
access, or agent runs on the user's own AI (NEED-4). No price number in the
repository.

## 4. Mechanism in brief

- **Entitlement.** `Org.Plan` is renamed `BilledPlan`; `EntitledPlan()`
  returns it while the billing status is none, trialing, active or past due,
  and the free tier otherwise; `EffectiveLimits()` reads the entitled plan,
  so every existing enforcement point follows without change. `past_due`
  keeps the paid plan with no local grace clock — Stripe's dunning terminal
  action (which must be cancel) is the grace period.
- **Flags.** `hosted_automation`, `teams` and `workspace_budget` join the
  limits catalogue as a boolean kind, resolved through the same three layers
  (workspace override, deployment, plan), so per-workspace grandfathering and
  the existing limits panel cover them for free.
- **Schema.** Migration 45 adds customer, subscription and item refs,
  currency, status, interval, seats, cancel-at-period-end, grandfathered,
  period end and synced-at to `organizations`, a trial-used timestamp to
  `users`, and unique partial indexes on the customer and subscription refs
  so one subscription can never entitle two workspaces.
- **Sync.** A reconcile loop lists every subscription from Stripe, matches
  by stored ref then by `metadata.openv_org_id`, applies each snapshot under
  a `plan_synced_at` guard, repairs seat drift, cancels subscriptions whose
  workspace is gone, and never changes a plan on a failed read. The
  post-checkout return page refreshes one workspace synchronously so the
  entitlement is live before it renders.
- **Endpoints.** Public plans catalogue (served from cache), workspace
  billing state, checkout, in-app plan change (one subscription per
  workspace), customer portal (no product switching), refresh. All workspace
  admin only; all registered unconditionally and answering 404 when billing
  is not configured.
- **Gates.** Unattended hosted compute at the hosted claim and hosted-runner
  creation (never at automation create, so a cron run claimed by the user's
  own worker stays free); people-teams at team creation and project-role
  grants; budget rollups at the workspace usage endpoint; seats and shared
  workspaces through the existing limit checks, with the shared-workspace
  count fixed to count creations rather than memberships; hosted minutes at
  lease creation from a monthly rollup of lease timings.
- **Lifecycle.** Soft delete cancels at period end (undone on restore);
  purge cancels immediately; the Stripe customer is never deleted. A
  platform-admin grant of enterprise or open source wins over a
  subscription. First bind writes a nightly release-channel override so a
  new subscriber does not lose every channel-gated feature.

## 5. Tier values when the numbers turn on (Phase 4)

| Plan | members | shared workspaces | projects | flags | hosted minutes/month |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| single / free | 2 | 1 | 200 (abuse) | all off | 300 |
| business_lite | 2 | 1 | 500 (abuse) | hosted_automation | unlimited |
| business / team / open_source | unlimited (billed per seat) | unlimited | 1000 (abuse) | all on | unlimited |
| enterprise / self_host | unlimited | unlimited | unlimited | all on | unlimited |

## 6. Requirements to record, per phase

Phase 1: entitlement resolved from plan and billing status (refining REQ-77,
REQ-123, DES-38); scheduled reconciliation that never downgrades on a failed
read; billing inert with no provider configured. Phase 2: the subscribe,
change-plan and manage-billing journeys; no payment card data handled by the
platform; the grandfathering promise with its date. Phase 3: per-seat
billing that never blocks a membership change. Phase 4: plan-limited members
and shared workspaces; read-only over plan with export always allowed (a test
case linked to REQ-113); the hosted-compute, teams and budget gates; the
hosted-minutes allowance.

## 7. Decisions for the maintainer

1. Merchant-of-record reality — tax registrations before the first charge.
2. Hand-rolled Stripe client versus `stripe-go` (recommendation: hand-rolled;
   reversible through the provider interface).
3. One Stripe customer per workspace (the unique index).
4. The grandfather date itself, to go in Phase 2's release notes.
5. Tax display exclusive of VAT; seat ceiling 500.

## 8. Review notes

An adversarial review of the draft found and the plan now corrects: a
deterministic seat-quantity idempotency key that Stripe would replay for 24
hours (7→8→7 sticks at 8); Lite being per-seat by accident; the teams gate
pointed at the agent-crews package; the hosted-compute gate placed at
automation creation where it would block runs on the user's own machine;
boot depending on Stripe being reachable; a new Business subscriber losing
every channel-gated feature on the plan flip; `checkSharedWorkspaceCount`
counting memberships; and missing handling for deletion, purge, enterprise
grants, re-subscribing, two admins checking out at once, portal plan
switches, currency lock, disputes and trial abuse.

product_profile.vision: OpenV is the multi-agent development suite that lets a solo founder (or a company) define products, manage requirements with full V&V traceability, and put AI agents to work as a real team - using each member's own AI subscription.
product_profile.problem_statement: Solo founders and small teams cannot afford dedicated requirements tooling plus a development team. Existing AI tools work from ad-hoc prompts with no traceability, no approval gates, and unpredictable execution that depends on whose laptop happens to be online.
product_profile.target_users: Solo founders defining and building products end-to-end; companies organizing requirements work across teams; external stakeholders contributing needs through interviews.

constraints.description: Consumer AI subscriptions (Claude/GPT/Gemini CLI logins) are personal-use: they run only on the member's own machine, never server-side. Company-wide AI is API-token only.
constraints.title: BYO-AI compliance

constraints.description: Provider API keys are never persisted in the database; worker keys, run tokens and pairing codes are stored as sha256 hashes with plaintext shown once.
constraints.title: No stored provider credentials

constraints.description: Nothing auto-starts on a member's machine; runners execute only while the user has the connector window open.
constraints.title: No background services on user machines

constraints.description: Agents receive requirements context exclusively from the requirements database and kanban history via tools, never from large prompt contexts or doc files.
constraints.title: Lean agent context

success_metrics.description: A founder can go from empty project to an agent-executed, human-approved change without leaving OpenV.
success_metrics.title: Definition to execution

success_metrics.description: Every requirement traces to a stakeholder need and is covered by at least one verification.
success_metrics.title: Full traceability

success_metrics.description: Queued agent runs start within the grace window whenever any eligible runner is available.
success_metrics.title: Predictable runs
